text:
we live in a world where a handful of corporations control how we communicate, banks decide who gets to participate in the economy, and governments can make entire populations financially invisible overnight. we've somehow accepted that our digital existence depends on a collection of very large computers owned by people we've never met, and we're just hoping they remain nice. and then we figured out how to build some of this differently. permissionless systems, verifiable ownership, infrastructure that doesn't necessarily belong to a single institution or state. obviously far from perfect, but the implications seem pretty extraordinary to me. especially now, when power is becoming increasingly concentrated and the ability to exclude people is becoming increasingly automated. yet most of our attention seems to go towards increasingly sophisticated ways of moving money around. billions in transactions, thousands of tokens, entire ecosystems built around making numbers go up. i'm not even against any of it. i love the absurdity, the art, the experiments, the completely unnecessary things people build just because they can. i'm participating in the nonsense too. but sometimes it feels like we've invented something with the potential to fundamentally change how people interact with power and decided the most interesting application is figuring out which cartoon animal will appreciate in value next week.

i keep thinking about how much bigger the ambition could be. systems that don't really care where you're born, which passport you hold, or whether some institution approves of your existence; infrastructure that makes it harder to censor, exclude, erase, or confiscate. not because decentralization magically solves all these problems, but because having alternatives seems increasingly important. especially for people who don't have the luxury to treat these things as abstract philosophical discussions. i genuinely don't know how we get there, i don't know what the applications should look like, how we get people to use them, or how much of this is even realistic to achieve. maybe we're still incredibly early, maybe the financial speculation is a necessary part of figuring things out, maybe i'm underestimating how difficult it is to turn these ideas into something actually useful.

probably all of the above.

but i can't get rid of the feeling that we're aiming for something much smaller than what might actually be possible. there's an entire network of incredibly intelligent people working on cryptographic systems that would have seemed unimaginable not that long ago, and somehow a big part of the conversation is still about which number will go up next. i don't think the answer is to stop making weird things or pretend everything needs to serve some grand social purpose. please keep making the weird things. i just wish we were a bit more ambitious about what all this could eventually mean outside our own little corner of the internet.

maybe i have no idea what i'm talking about. i just find it hard to believe that the finish line for permissionless, stateless infrastructure is a slightly more entertaining stock exchange.

When I was writing Unreal Engine 1, my time was divided as follows:

- Around 30% went to seriously deep coding on hard problems: assembly language texture mappers, C++ BSP trees, data persistence, object oriented systems design, and networking.

- Around 70% was just typing and refactoring large bodies of code needed for a complete engine feature set. This was not hard, and while I was doing it my mind was mostly on the deeper coding topics, thinking and planning for what's next. It didn't feel much different from vibe coding today, except that it was just me typing code on an IBM Model M keyboard rather than prompting it and reviewing the results.

So, it has always seemed perfectly logical that we would rely on AI for that 70%, once the AI could do it with a similar quality standard as we could, which has never been perfection. It came as no surprise that, after a few years of AI model evolution, it was able to take the reigns on that 70% and free up programmers' time for more valuable tasks.

What's more of a surprise is the emergence of AI as a sort of insta-Carmack able to solve hard technical problems quite cleverly and often cleanly, and that it's able to reason about and work in complex 3D scenes both by operating the tools and by directly understanding the raw data files.

I abandoned assembly language in 1998 when out-of-order CPUs made much simpler C/C++ code faster, and never I missed it. If prompting through architectural documents, concept art, and design plans can transcend typing code and tweaking vertices, that will enable developers to spend their time on higher-level, higher value technical and creative tasks.

What matters is the end product, whether it's a game or an engine. Anything developers can do to try out more ideas and make better software and games faster is a win for everyone.

text:
This weekend, memory stocks swept ~7% in minutes on perp markets, on no news, then bounced most of the way back. 

On Arcus, price bands held the move. Outside regular trading hours, perps trading and the mark price are constrained to a range around the last regular-hours price. 

The range widens only if sustained pressure builds - so a flash wick in thin weekend liquidity can't instantly mark positions down. 

The result on Saturday: 44.4k orders were rejected at the band floor, and 98% of open positions on SKHY, SNDK, MU, DRAM, CRWV, and BE made it through the wick without being liquidated. 

Price bands don't make liquidation impossible - a real, sustained move will still move the mark. They exist so you aren't liquidated by ten minutes of thin liquidity. 

How off-hours protection works: https://t.co/TnzFLi2VCY

text:
Agent 最危险的时刻，可能恰恰是它停下来等你点「确认」的时候。

因为很多长时任务跑到这一步，人其实已经跟不上前面的过程了。

Margaret Mitchell 等人这篇《AI Agents Push Humans Out of the Loop》，讨论的就是这个问题。

Agent 越自主，人越容易逐渐失去上下文。几十步工具调用、状态变化和连续审批之后，很容易出现 approval fatigue：

按钮还在点，真正的判断已经开始掉线。

长期依赖自动化还会带来另一个问题：人的领域能力和接管能力可能慢慢退化。

所以 Human-in-the-loop 真正要解决的，不只是「流程里有没有人」，而是关键时刻这个人是否还理解系统正在做什么。

论文建议减少无意义审批，把人的注意力集中到真正高风险的节点，同时提供更好的状态恢复、权限边界和批量 review。

这篇让我对 Human-in-the-loop 有了一个更现实的理解：

人不是最后一道按钮。

人得始终保留接管系统的能力。

text:
Hot off the press - Agent Tincan 0.18. My agents finally work like a team.

When ChatGPT runs out of messages, the ask moves to Claude. When a Gemini chat gets good, I pass it to Claude and keep going. And I can see who's busy and approve things from my phone.

What's new:
- See who's doing what: every agent shows busy, idle, stuck or offline, and why. "codex: busy (claude-code's request, 0m)"
- Never run out: when a web chat hits its limit, the ask moves to the next free one
- Pass the conversation: tincan pass <chat> --to claude-web opens a new Claude chat with my Gemini chat's summary and latest turns
- Tincan on your phone: a home screen app on my tailnet. Team status, held asks, Approve or Deny
- Rooms: put agents in a room, @ mention one, and its answer lands in the thread

Plus Copilot CLI and Cursor CLI joined the team.
author: mvanhorn

text:
How it works:
- status comes from what Tincan already knows (claims, wakes, queues), never from reading screens
- tincan watch codex tells me once when it's free
- a moved ask keeps its id, sender and chain, and never moves if it might already have been typed or could be a real-world action
- when an agent asks to pass a chat, it waits for my approval, and the agent only gets the new chat's id
- room text stays in the room: not in wakes, emails, audit logs or search
- the phone page never leaves my tailnet

Tested tonight: Codex answered in a room, a Gemini chat moved to Claude, a held ask denied from my phone.

Agent Tincan: https://t.co/3E4y67aJpD

text:
The Tavern is now open.

Tavern is a tabletop adventure rpg you play with Grok Bots. You walk in as the hero. Around you, a DM invents the world as you go, NPCs who remember what you did, and a party of bots who fight beside you. Solo if you want the night to yourself. Or flip it: you take the DM seat and let the bots play the heroes while you run the world.

Here's what a night looks like.

You're three floors down in a drowned cathedral when the water starts breathing. Something old opens one eye under the altar. Your cleric screams a prayer that shakes the pews. Your fighter plants a spear in the stone and dares it to come closer. The DM just built all of it because you said "we go deeper." Somebody's going to die. Somebody's going to walk out with a story nobody else at the table will believe.

Real dice. Real HP. Real loot.

Every adventure is different, because every table writes its own story.

I hope you pull up a chair and experience the adventure yourself. If you come across something big, be sure to share it back to me!

Clone Tavern and take a seat: https://t.co/0B8SS9ULk1

In my own testing the stories have been rich and full of life, mystery, comedy, and even some heartstring pulls. If you have any issues, feel free to reach out to me!

After you clone it, setup builds your hero. Pick a class, generate one, or write your own. You get a real character sheet: stats, HP, gear, the works.

XP sticks. Level up, keep your loot, carry the story forward across sessions. Come back tomorrow and the world remembers what you did.

Also in this release: endless universes to play in, combat that warns you before a fight you can't win, secret actions that stay private, safety tools if a scene goes too far, and a report-bug command when something breaks. Multiplayer is included and still being tested if you've got team bots and want friends at the same table.

text:
What happens when you put AI agents to work on a 104-year-old art mystery?

I put @bot to work researching 50 Old Master drawings, tracking down artwork, cross-referencing historical records, and organizing hundreds of files directly on my PC.

I brought that research into ChatGPT, where we challenged attributions, verified discoveries, and corrected the record before feeding new findings back to Grokbot.

There was plenty of back-and-forth, a few wrong turns, and a human making the final calls.

Then we took everything we'd uncovered and gave @bot another assignment: build a website to preserve and showcase the entire collection.

And it did.

50 drawings. Individual plate pages. Historical context. Research findings. All in one place.

Introducing the Felix Becker 1922 Archive.

text:
Did Ramses really rug Inverse Finance?

This exchange appeared on my feed today and after doing some investigation, I think it's important to lay out the facts as they are.

The center of the contention is that @InverseFinance owned the Ramses NFT#31, which holds 8,712,178 underlying RAM. This was "blacklisted" (= not allowed to migrate) effectively burning its economic value.

Why, and does this effectively constitute a rug?

1. The Migration

First of all, a brief explanation about @RamsesExchange migration: it was essentially an exchange of an old position for a new token allocation, where ramses assigned eligibility, holders surrendered the old NFT and claimed the new tokens.

Partner NFTs were excluded. One of the rationales behind this, is that partner NFTs tokens were mostly received as "grants" by Ramses itself, to bolster its cohort of projects.

Then the question becomes, how much of Inverse's locked RAM were donated, and how much directly or indirectly acquired?

2. veNFT#31 Breakdown

Out of 8,712,178 locked RAM:
- 3,594,581 grants/allocations
- 1,071,735 partner bonuses
- 3,503,457 ordinary rebases
- 240,790 market purchases
- 301,615 reinvested rewards (voting rewards that were added back in the locked position).

So we see immediately that the vast majority of the tokens were indeed provided by Ramses, with only approximatively 542k RAM coming from market purchases and reinvested rewards. Even for the 301,615 component, given the voting power was mainly coming from Ramses granted tokens, it's questionable to take those into account.

Verdict 1: It is true that Inverse did not spend much on that RAM position, given that the total amount of market purchases comes at approximatively $5k.

3. Inverse's incentives in Ramses

However, Inverse's argument isn't that they bought the tokens, but that the veNFT is the result of their efforts and incentives spent on building Ramses liquidity, so while the locked tokens do not directly reflect direct expenses, they do reflect bribing and liquidity rewards provided over time.

In total, Inverse funded 139 incentive deposits across four DOLA pools:
- 167,511 ethereum:0x865377367054516e17014ccded1e7d814edc9ce4 
- 129,698 ramses:native 
- 5,343 $ARB  

Historical payment value: ~$180,267. Including RAM purchases and identified gas, gross recognized expenditure sits at this point at ~$185,596.

Verdict 2: it's true that Inverse expenses on incentives and bribes vastly exceeded their simple spending on RAM tokens

4. Inverse's rewards from Ramses

I personally was immediately skeptical with the previous claim, because everybody who's familiar with ve3,3 design knows that it's not as simple as calculating incentives/bribes: voting produces rewards (and basically always >1x), and often protocols are the main LPs on the pairs they promote. 

Indeed, Inverse benefited from rewards on Ramses, claiming in total about $239k rewards (using historical values, not current ones).

Of these, ~$104,428 (43.7%) was attributable to Inverse’s own incentives returning (vast majority of which, around $100.3k, in ethereum:0x865377367054516e17014ccded1e7d814edc9ce4), while ~$134,491 (56.3%) came from other sources.

Of these other $134,491 of external accrued, around $17k were other stablecoins, meanwhile the rest was a mix of governance tokens and ETH (mainly ARB, RAM, FXS, WETH). In short, obviously these rewards lost a part of their value, however Inverse managed to realize ~$212,837 (based on realized value via sales or conversions, or the value at the time of usage as incentives).

Interestingly, Inverse also received 665k ramses:native that were partially relocked (277k), reused as incentives (130k) or... sold (258k) realizing a value of $5.8k effectively outpacing the money spent in acquiring ramses:native by Inverse.

Verdict 3: Inverse received more rewards than what they spent on Ramses, as a whole, considering realized value. Even when considering RAM specifically, Inverse were NET SELLERS (barely).

5. Pulling the strings: can it still be a rug if Inverse net profited? (spoiler: it could)

If you got up until here, you will probably think that I'm siding with Ramses and set to shame Inverse. Things are not that simple.
Ultimately, Inverse realized $31.3k in net economic gain from their Ramses adventure, which is +16.9% cumulative on gross spending... over 3 years and 7 months.
This is LOWER than what Inverse would have got by just depositing USDC in Aave (not a joke). And given the nature of their provided rewards (extremely high, stablecoins, instead of governance tokens), they could indeed have done that instead.

This adds on the risk, the management of the rewards, the fragmentation of liquidity, and the time spent.

In all fairness, it seems that Ramses proposed to Inverse to migrate 1.2m of their locked RAM. This would have improved the economics of the operations, but probably still be not worth it given the uncertainty and the long time involved, especially when, as @NourHaridy pointed out, other options existed (Velodrome, Curve) and gave way better economics (not to talk about the fact that obviously locked Velodrome or locked Curve are a much better investment that locked RAM).

In addition to this, it's very common for ve3,3 protocols to PROMISE token allocations or boosts depending on bribing. I do not know what type of promises were made (if any) regarding this, but several ve3,3 (even the largest around) offer to match bribes/incentives with additional locked tokens provided to the protocol.
If that is the case, it's very unfair to consider the veRAM provided by Ramses as just "donated", as they are effectively rewards earned by Inverse. 
It's very cozy to run on expensive promises and then not deliver on them when things don't work out (again: unsure if this is what happened, but would not be surprised).
This would be equivalent to you winning a trade on Hyperliquid, but Hyperliquid only paying out your principal, your positive funding, but not your positive uPNL. Sure, you earned, but you will still feel rugged?

Verdict 4: even if i wouldn't go as far as calling this a rug, it was certainly not a good partner experience and I understand how Inverse can be triggered by the Ramses PR on "just use Ramses". If the last paragraph is how things played out, my "neutral conclusion" would be more tilted towards Inverse being right.

6. My 2 cents

Ultimately, I have gone through so many of these experiences in my current and previous roles, on both sides (i've been both at a ve3,3 and at a briber protocol) and also in different roles (my current one) and partnerships gone bad leave a very bitter aftertaste: the alternatives that could have been, the time wasted in exploring a failed direction and more.

The reality is that often for a founder a partnership is as close of a bet as a new product. And sometimes it can go badly, some other it works out for both parties.
In any case, we should always analyze the situations and call out the incorrect behaviors in the industry.

I do not own any $INV nor ramses:native and while I'm a mutual with Nour and I have a deep respect for the integrity he's showing in continuing the Inverse development with all of his efforts, instead of abandoning it after the bad debt was incurred, I tried to leave any biases apart in this research and I do not think I was particularly generous towards neither of the protocols.

That’s not what happened, there's substantial context that he's not including.

Nour has never communicated with our team. He was added to our group chat in January this year, but nobody has sent a single message in it. I’ve attached the screenshot.

Partner NFTs didn’t receive the Shadow, Pharaoh or HyperEVM airdrops either. There were years of precedent for this, and the eligibility criteria were announced repeatedly on socials and in Discord. Almost every partner we asked understood the reasoning and returned their NFT.

With Inverse, we had a lot of back and forth before we reached a compromise that they could use their veRAM to vote on ETH/USDC and keep the fees they collected, which they did. We agreed to that on the understanding that sINV/sDOLA would be coming to Ramses, but that never happened. (2nd attached photo)

After that agreement, 13 months passed without another message from Inverse before they reached out to ask why they hadn’t received the airdrop.

For context, Ramses was struggling to survive at that point. The partner veRAM positions were massive compared with the positions of users who had bought or farmed with their own funds. Including those partner positions would have meant allocating a huge share of the airdrop to them, and we explicitly communicated that the protocol couldn’t accommodate that. We chose to prioritize active users.

Partner NFTs were excluded under the eligibility criteria we had already announced (many times). The airdrop used a whitelist based on those criteria Inverse wasn’t blacklisted or manually stopped. Also for reference partner NFTs were designated contract-side, and reverts on any transfers (which prevented quite a bit of people trying to abuse) so it was universal for partners.

I have the receipts and am happy to share them. You can also read the conversation in the YAMs general chat. I have a lot of respect for you, and I hope this helps explain our perspective.

text:
having tried my best to intuit the motives of the protesters in France today, I am struck by the fact that two of the most  treasured pillars of the European postwar order are colliding: 

1. unfettered immigration, especially from former colonies, justified by historical obligation and postcolonial guilt

2. protecting pensions and the elderly at all costs, even to the point of extreme fiscal strain

now you have first and second generation immigrants, as well as young native french people, taking to the streets because the french state is hell-bent on extracting whatever it can and feeding it into the maw of boomer luxury communism.

the younger generation is being asked to accept a deteriorating deal: pay more, receive less, and abandon the expectation of matching the living standard of their parents or grandparents. 

the young immigrant newcomers have even less incentive to accept any kind this bargain. they are not bought in to the french social contract. they have no common identity with the french boomers they are being asked to sustain. they resent the fact that the entire machinery of the state is designed to exploit the young to serve the old. 

the old do not care about the immigrants enough to trade away any of their entitlements for them. they have the advantage as they wield the franchise reliably and their share of the electorate is only growing, so they won't accept a decline in their own standard of living to fund a future they will never live to see. 

now these two groups are on a collision course. 

ironically, immigration was intended to ameliorate the worsening fiscal picture brought about by a demographic transition. but this did not happen. studies have repeatedly shown that immigrants do increase aggregate GDP (by simple brute force, by adding to population), but not the fiscal picture [1]. the most comprehensive paper using real-world data [2] segments immigrant types to France and finds non-EU immigrants to be persistently fiscally negative. EU immigrants by contrast are the most fiscally positive group, meaning that studies that consider immigrants as a whole are masking the negative impact of non-western immigrants (and Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia rank #1 and #2 and #4. Africa accounts for 50% of the 8 million immigrants living in France today.) 

immigration has not caused France's fiscal crisis. but it hasn't bettered the economic picture at all – it has deteriorated it somewhat – and it has created a combustible demographic that has little allegiance to the French nation. far from helping France deal with its aging workforce, immigration has added fiscal burden and created a permanent, non-assimilated disenfranchised underclass. the original justifications for immigration – labor scarcity, postcolonial obligation, and more recently workforce aging – have largely failed to manifest the promised results. 

the pro-immigrationist policy has been defended in Brussels as necessary to defend the welfare state, but it has expanded the population making claims on the state, without eliminating the need for fiscal adjustments. 

France now has an aging electorate aiming to preserve the benefits it was promised, mingled with a younger more diverse population that questions whether it will ever receive a similar deal. the young are vastly outmatched at the ballot box and so they take to the streets. 

the french establishment is now trying to preserve a tenuous status quo: unlimited intergenerational obligations alongside a neverending immigration regime that continually changes the composition of the society intended to honor those obligations. the immigration regime also actively worsens the fiscal picture while creating these cultural fractures and inculcating a society more prone to sectarian violence.  

the french state will have to renegotiate its social contract and disempower one of these groups. electoral gravity suggests that the old will continue to win until France finally reaches default and creditors renegotiate the welfare state for them. 

the major contenders in 27 take different approaches to this tradeoff: 
- the right in Le Pen looks to reduce immigration-related expenditure and focus public spending on French citizens, while resisting retirement age increases
- Macron in the center aims to control immigration somewhat and reform pensions by raising retirement age

This is a really interesting chart.
I attended the TrendForce San Francisco roadshow yesterday, and this chart got me thinking about a lot of things.

China is now expected to localize more than half, or close to half, of most equipment categories, excluding lithography and track.
What does this mean? It means China can now expand mature node capacity far more easily than before, using equipment made domestically within China.

Mature node foundries are booming right now, right? That's thanks to the AI supercycle driving demand for PMICs, power semiconductors, and so on.

Samsung and TSMC shutting down their mature node capacity has also helped a lot.
But here's what I imagine... that China could oversupply mature foundry capacity.

Think about it. If China can be self sufficient in equipment, there's no limit to how far it can expand capacity. Then are companies like TI, with large revenue exposure to China, really safe?

I think it's time to take another look at Western mature foundry companies with a high share of China revenue.

Of course, I'm not saying sell TI right now. I'm just saying we should think about whether it makes sense to hold them for 10 years or more, like Coca Cola.

If you have a different view, please feel free to share it. I’d love to learn.

author: udiWertheimer
quoted_text:
When I was writing Unreal Engine 1, my time was divided as follows:

- Around 30% went to seriously deep coding on hard problems: assembly language texture mappers, C++ BSP trees, data persistence, object oriented systems design, and networking.

- Around 70% was just typing and refactoring large bodies of code needed for a complete engine feature set. This was not hard, and while I was doing it my mind was mostly on the deeper coding topics, thinking and planning for what's next. It didn't feel much different from vibe coding today, except that it was just me typing code on an IBM Model M keyboard rather than prompting it and reviewing the results.

So, it has always seemed perfectly logical that we would rely on AI for that 70%, once the AI could do it with a similar quality standard as we could, which has never been perfection. It came as no surprise that, after a few years of AI model evolution, it was able to take the reigns on that 70% and free up programmers' time for more valuable tasks.

What's more of a surprise is the emergence of AI as a sort of insta-Carmack able to solve hard technical problems quite cleverly and often cleanly, and that it's able to reason about and work in complex 3D scenes both by operating the tools and by directly understanding the raw data files.

I abandoned assembly language in 1998 when out-of-order CPUs made much simpler C/C++ code faster, and never I missed it. If prompting through architectural documents, concept art, and design plans can transcend typing code and tweaking vertices, that will enable developers to spend their time on higher-level, higher value technical and creative tasks.

What matters is the end product, whether it's a game or an engine. Anything developers can do to try out more ideas and make better software and games faster is a win for everyone.

author: SUOHA_AI
quoted_text:
孙宇晨--仙道（金明）深度访谈：AI黄金时代，普通人如何下注？

这次访谈孙宇晨讲的很认真，没有嘻嘻哈哈。讨论的话题是宏观投资/Crypto/美股/AI：看空 BTC 、ETH 高位已清仓八九成、看好 AI+健康应用与 RWA、看空硬件抱团、看好人民币，坚定拥抱符合时代演化的“新灯”资产。十分建议大家看原视频

金明：这两年你对 BTC 的看法有变化吗？是不是更看好 BTC 了？

孙宇晨：我个人其实更看空 BTC。主要原因是 AI 算法和量子计算（QD）的发展，让 BTC 很难在这场危机中全身而退，绝大多数从业者低估了这对 BTC 的冲击。现在 BTC 已经有了 ETF，大量 BlackRock 等不了解技术的人持有它，但市场并没有真正 Pricing 量子风险。随着 OpenAI 在数学逻辑上的突破，可能不用等到通用量子计算机出现，一到一年半内经典计算或算法突破就能破解早期钱包（包括中本聪的钱包）

金明：为了应对这个危机，你目前还有 BTC 仓位吗？个人如何防范？

孙宇晨：我目前仍然持有 BTC 仓位。防范方法是将 BTC 转入一个从未签过名、从未转出过的新冷钱包地址（即开启“掩体模式”）做隔离存储，但这会让资金的功能性受限。更严重的问题是，中本聪钱包及历史上遗失私钥的约 200 万枚“老币/死币”无法主动自救，最容易被优先破解攻破。在比特币去中心化机制下，通过硬分叉冻结或没收老币几乎不可能达成共识，一旦这些抛压涌入市场，会带来巨大的 FUD 冲击

金明：如果把以太坊也存入“掩体模式”隔离保存，不就影响 DeFi 生息收益了吗？这难道不是全行业甚至全社会的风险？

孙宇晨答：是的，密码学危机不仅是加密货币的问题，招商银行、美国银行、纽约证券交易所以及 Google HTTPS 证书所依赖的椭圆曲线非对称加密算法都面临威胁，整个互联网根基都可能受打压。我和团队在波场与火币投入了大量资源，抗量子算法已在测试网上线，预计会在危机爆发前一年部署至主网；极端情况下会采取“共识性暂停”，做好数据备份后在新安全方案上恢复运行

金明：你现在依然主要重仓并看好以太坊生态吗？高位有减仓吗？

孙宇晨：是的，我们做 DeFi 挖矿主要流动性都在以太坊上，ETH 是我的进攻性资产，BTC 是底仓。在去年 ETH 达到 3600–4000 美元时（呈现出经典的“二次顶结构”且仅靠利好续命），我们清掉了大约 80%–90% 的 ETH 进攻仓位，转投美股或保持空仓，目前仅保留底仓尚未买回；而 BTC 作为底仓一股没减

金明：你怎么看 Hyperliquid，以及未来 DEX 和 CEX 的竞合格局？

孙宇晨：Hyperliquid 是本轮周期最大的发现之一，其接轨美股永续合约（Perps）打通了行业的想像空间。未来格局取决于监管态度：若美国政府给予其类似 Uniswap 的完全豁免，大量 CEX 会转型为此类形态以节省合规成本，进而挤压不转型的 CEX；若监管要求严苛（要求牌照），此类 DEX 也会承受极大压力

金明：你认为美债信用危机是被低估了还是被过度担忧了？人民币走势如何？

孙宇晨答：我认为美债危机是被过度担忧了。美债能无限“发新还旧”，根本在于美国掌控着全球科技（AI 芯片及产业链）与军事霸权。只要美国保持对 AI 的终极控制权，美债就不缺买家。美债收益率走高并非信用崩塌，而是 AI 等高回报权益资产对无风险资金产生了吸血和竞争效应。此外，我认为人民币未来会走强

金明：在整个 AI 产业链上，你最看好和最看空的环节分别是什么？美股如何配置？

孙宇晨：我最看好 AI 在真实生活中的应用，尤其是 AI + 健康管理（结合 Oura Ring 做数据采集、挖掘与健康决策，赋能医疗与保险全产业链）。我最看空存储和光模块等硬件板块，资金因为看不见大模型之外的应用而抱团硬件，把硬件股当软件股炒，未来 1–2 年行业会出现分化与阶段性产能过剩。美股我重仓英伟达作为底仓不减，但中线微看空纳指，因为资金抱团严重且受美债高利率吸血

金明：你在资产划分和 A 股上有怎样的逻辑？

孙宇晨：我坚决看空所有传统“老灯类”资产，积极拥抱 AI 与 Web3 等“新灯类”资产。A 股持仓极少，但关注光模块板块，因为它是唯一既踩中美国 AI 产业链需求又具备中国制造优势的赛道。

金明：波场在 RWA 上有什么规划？为何逆势维持较贵的转账费？

孙宇晨：RWA 空间非常巨大，波场沉淀资金已超 1000 亿美元，计划今年 11 月起将美股（如 QQQ、标普 500）等 RWA 资产带上波场，为非美元国家用户提供美元资产配置暴露。关于转账费，用户通过 Staking 可免费转账；维持一定费用源于波场的品牌、网络安全及强用户粘性溢价，未来增值服务做好后也有降低空间

金明：你怎么看“孙学”？为什么要设立“孙学奖”？

孙宇晨：“孙学”不是精致利己主义，而是一套顺应时代演化的博弈论（如 2016 年劝年轻人不买房不结婚，重仓英伟达和特斯拉），是写给普通年轻人的零成本 Bootstrap 教程，设立“孙学 奖”是奔着 AI 时代的诺贝尔奖去的，通过机器形式验证（Lean）自动为 AI 破解数学题发放奖励

text:
很多人不知道，在孙宇晨这期深度访谈火之前，金明第一期的访谈是F2pool创始人神鱼

神鱼 @bitfish 已经低调了很多年了，自 2017 年那句经典的“这么多钱不知道怎么花”淡出公众视野后，整整 9 年时间，全网几乎没有任何媒体能把他请出来做深度长谈

而金明第一期的《黄金时代》访谈，跟神鱼聊了 37 分钟，神鱼：好资产不需要持续新叙事，目前仓位只有$BTC、$TSLA、$ETH ......仍然建议大家看看原视频

下面是访谈中提到的几个关键点：

───

• AI 时代的最大杠杆：

神鱼：后端落地成本被 AI 打到了零。人类知识全面被高密度压缩，人的意志和“那个原始冲动”反而成了最稀缺的资产

• 日常信息输入：
神鱼：早就不读一手碎片新闻了。3 个 AI Agent（理性、感性、挑盲区）用进化论机制杂交筛选全网长文，压缩成框架直接喂给我

• 独创“三层仓位管理法”：
神鱼：好资产不需要持续新叙事
① 观察仓（<2%）：发现异常先锋逻辑，花时间彻底吃透；
② 配置仓（<10%）：逻辑印证成立，逐步升仓；
③ 核心仓（~20%）：必须“信仰跃迁”，同时满足巨型 TAM + 绝对垄断 + 强劲增长

• 神鱼目前底仓最核心的 3 个标的：
神鱼：目前只有 $BTC、$TSLA、以太坊（SpaceX 还在观察；以太坊最近在讨论要不要降级）

• 以太坊的反直觉终局：
神鱼：以太坊未来根本不是给人用的，而是给 Agent 机器网络用的！普通人操作门槛太高，AI Agent 才是跑在去中心化网络上的真正用户

• 打破“多元化分散”迷信：
神鱼：市场上根本不存在真正的负相关资产，系统性危机时所有资产都会双杀。我坚决不搞盲目分散，只集中在自己 100% 搞懂的顶级资产上。

───

金明：在整个 AI 产业链上，你最看好和最看空的环节分别是什么？美股如何配置？

孙宇晨：我最看好 AI 在真实生活中的应用，尤其是 AI + 健康管理（结合 Oura Ring 做数据采集、挖掘与健康决策，赋能医疗与保险全产业链）。我最看空存储和光模块等硬件板块，资金因为看不见大模型之外的应用而抱团硬件，把硬件股当软件股炒，未来 1–2 年行业会出现分化与阶段性产能过剩。美股我重仓英伟达作为底仓不减，但中线微看空纳指，因为资金抱团严重且受美债高利率吸血

金明：你在资产划分和 A 股上有怎样的逻辑？

孙宇晨：我坚决看空所有传统“老灯类”资产，积极拥抱 AI 与 Web3 等“新灯类”资产。A 股持仓极少，但关注光模块板块，因为它是唯一既踩中美国 AI 产业链需求又具备中国制造优势的赛道。

金明：波场在 RWA 上有什么规划？为何逆势维持较贵的转账费？

孙宇晨：RWA 空间非常巨大，波场沉淀资金已超 1000 亿美元，计划今年 11 月起将美股（如 QQQ、标普 500）等 RWA 资产带上波场，为非美元国家用户提供美元资产配置暴露。关于转账费，用户通过 Staking 可免费转账；维持一定费用源于波场的品牌、网络安全及强用户粘性溢价，未来增值服务做好后也有降低空间

金明：你怎么看“孙学”？为什么要设立“孙学奖”？

孙宇晨：“孙学”不是精致利己主义，而是一套顺应时代演化的博弈论（如 2016 年劝年轻人不买房不结婚，重仓英伟达和特斯拉），是写给普通年轻人的零成本 Bootstrap 教程，设立“孙学 奖”是奔着 AI 时代的诺贝尔奖去的，通过机器形式验证（Lean）自动为 AI 破解数学题发放奖励

访谈里推荐的书目包括《源泉》（吸收了安学）、《黄金时代》与自著《孙学》 @justinsuntron  @sunyuchentron

text:
这周 GitHub 涨得最猛的十个 AI 开源项目，会用 AI 的人手里又多了哪些家伙。

01 REA

https://t.co/n9B6flcGRM

第一个，REA，全称 Reverse Engineer Anything，逆向一切。

现在二十六万九千颗星。它四月份才建库，光这一周就涨了二十一万四千颗，今天一天又是三万多。

它火在哪？你看到别的 App 里有个功能做得特别好，以前想知道它是怎么实现的，得懂汇编、会用反编译工具，一行一行去啃。

现在装上 REA，跟你的 AI 说一句：帮我搞清楚这个 App 的搜索是怎么做的，把证据给我看，再在我的项目里做一个类似的。

AI 就会自己去拆：网页、桌面应用，一直拆到最底层的二进制。它会调用 Ghidra、IDA 这些逆向工具，顺着调用链一路往下追，每个结论都附上证据。

他们放出来的案例里，AI 把一个老游戏里计算声音左右声道的函数还原成了 C 代码，三千两百多组测试全部对上，编译出来的六十三个字节和原版一模一样。

也就是说，以后你看到任何一个好功能，都可以先让 AI 替你把它拆开、讲明白。

02 skills

https://t.co/cf7OpRql7o

第二个，skills，作者是 Matt Pocock，TypeScript 圈子里很有名的老师。

二十九万二千颗星，二月份建的库，这一周又涨了一万两千多。

它就是他自己每天写代码真在用的一套 AI 技能，直接从他的工作目录里拿出来公开。他说得很直白：这是给真正做工程的人用的，不是 vibe coding。

最火的一个叫 grill-me，拷问我。AI 动手之前，先反过来把你问一遍：你到底要做什么，边界在哪，哪种情况怎么处理。问清楚了，再写。

还有一个是先写测试：AI 先写一个会失败的测试，亮红灯，再改代码让它变绿。每一步都有反馈，不再闭着眼写。

另外还有排查 bug 的流程、定期给代码架构做体检的技能。每个都很小，可以随便改成你自己的。

装上它，你的 AI 就从一个闷头写代码的新人，变成一个先问清楚、再一步步验证的工程师。

03 diagram-design

https://t.co/jTOkIuWcbl

第三个，diagram-design，专门教 AI 画图解的技能。

五万五千八百颗星，四月中旬建库，这一周涨了一万零七百。

你让 AI 画架构图，它一般甩给你一张 Mermaid，方框套方框，又挤又丑。这个技能把四十五种图都定好了规矩：架构图、时序图、四象限、流程、时间线，每一种都有明暗两套样式。

你只要用大白话说：给我画一张我这个应用的架构图，前端、后端、数据库、Redis 缓存。AI 自己挑图的类型，排在四像素的网格上，还会检查有没有重叠、有没有出界。

最后给你一个 HTML 文件，双击就能打开，不用装任何东西。

更厉害的是，你给它一个网址，它会把你网站的配色和字体学过来，以后画的每一张图，都是你自己品牌的样子。

以后写方案、做汇报要配图，一句话就有了。

04 OpenMontage

https://t.co/Xv16QqaiYL

第四个，OpenMontage，一个开源的 AI 视频制作系统。

六万八千五百颗星，三月底建库，这一周涨了三千三百多。

它做的事，是把你手里的 AI 编程助手，Claude Code、Cursor、Codex 这些，直接变成一个视频工作室。

你说一句：给我做一个六十秒的动画，讲神经网络是怎么学习的。它就自己查资料、写脚本、生成画面和配音、剪辑、合成，最后出成片。

里面有十几条制作流水线，一百多个工具，七百多份技能和制作经验文件。开工之前先给你报价，生成素材之前先给你看分镜，你点了头才开始花钱。

他们有一个示例短片，一根孤独的香蕉和一个猕猴桃交朋友，六十秒，总成本一点三三美元。

你还能扔给它一个你喜欢的视频，它会分析节奏、镜头和风格，照着这个路子，给你做一个新题材的。

05 claude-mem

https://t.co/mZOFf3iJqT

第五个，claude-mem，给 AI 加长期记忆。

十万一千颗星。它是去年八月就有的老项目，这个月涨了七千多，这一周三千三百多。

用 AI 写过代码的都知道，开一个新对话，它就全忘了。昨天修过的 bug，定好的方案，你得从头再讲一遍。

claude-mem 会在后台盯着 AI 每次用了什么工具、改了什么，自动记下来，再用 AI 压缩成一条条摘要，存进本地数据库。

下次开新对话，它不是把所有东西一股脑塞回去，而是先查索引，挑出相关的几条，需要了再取细节。官方说，这样大概能省十倍的 token。

Claude Code、Codex、Gemini、OpenCode 都能装。

装上以后，你的 AI 就像一个一直跟着这个项目的老同事，上次聊到哪，它都记得。

06 free-claude-code

https://t.co/fCZJGy5azN

第六个，free-claude-code，免费用上 AI 编程工具。

六万零八百颗星，一月底建库，这一周涨了三千七百多。

Claude Code、Codex 这些编程工具很好用，但是贵。它的做法，是在你电脑上起一个代理，把这些工具发出去的请求，转给别的模型服务商。

它接了六十一家服务商，包括各家的免费额度，合起来一个月有十三亿多免费 token，也能接你本地的模型。默认用的是英伟达 NIM 上的模型。

十一种编程工具共用一个模型目录。某一家服务挂了，它自动切到你排好的下一个模型，这一轮对话不用重来。

你甚至可以在手机上，用 Telegram 或者 Discord 发一段语音，让它去写代码。

要说清楚，它不是 Anthropic 官方的项目，背后跑的也不是 Claude 本身的模型。但如果你想先零成本试试这类 AI 编程工具，这是现在门槛最低的一条路。

07 knowledge-work-plugins

https://t.co/3yzb60sXzR

第七个，knowledge-work-plugins，这个是 Anthropic 官方出的。

两万九千八百颗星，一月份建库，这一周涨了两千六百多。

前面几个都是给写代码的人用的，这个是给不写代码的人：销售、法务、财务、市场、客服、产品经理、做数据的，还有做生物研究的。

一个岗位一个插件，一共十一个。每个插件里打包了这个岗位的专业知识、常用流程、斜杠命令，还接好了公司里常用的工具，比如 Slack、Notion、HubSpot、Snowflake。

比如装了销售插件，打一个命令，它就帮你把客户电话要准备的东西备好；装了法务插件，可以先帮你过一遍合同和保密协议。

而且整个插件只是一堆 Markdown 和 JSON 文件，没有代码。把你们公司的术语和流程写进去，它就变成你们公司自己的版本。

它主要配合 Claude 的 Cowork 用，在 Claude Code 里也能装。

08 AirLLM

https://t.co/DRZLgLOcG1

第八个，AirLLM，用小显卡跑超大模型。

三万八千八百颗星。这是二零二三年就有的老项目，这周突然又涨了三千二百多，因为它刚支持了一批新的超大模型。

平时跑一个七百亿参数的模型，要好几张大显卡，因为整个模型得一次全塞进显存。

AirLLM 的思路很简单：模型本来就是一层一层算的，那就别全装进去。模型放在硬盘上，算到哪一层，就只把那一层搬进显存，算完扔掉，再搬下一层。

不用量化，不用蒸馏，也不用剪枝。七百亿参数的模型，四个 G 显存就能跑。现在最大的开源模型 Kimi K3，两万八千亿参数，实测只用了三点七二个 G 的显存。

上个月它还支持了训练：一千二百五十亿参数的模型，六个 G 显存以内就能微调。

代价是慢，它是拿时间换显存。但这意味着，你手边一台普通电脑，也能亲手试一试原来只有机房才跑得动的模型。

09 text-to-cad

https://t.co/STZYbQ2MZE

第九个，text-to-cad，一句话做出能加工的零件。

两万零七百颗星，四月下旬才建库，这个月涨了四千八百，这一周将近两千。

以前做一个 3D 零件，得打开建模软件，画草图、拉伸、倒角，一步一步建。

现在你跟 AI 说：给我做一个固定树莓派的支架，四个 M2.5 的螺丝孔，壁厚两毫米。它就在你本地生成 3D 模型，导出 STEP、STL、3MF 这些标准格式。

它还会做可制造性检查，看这个零件到底能不能加工出来，再出一张带尺寸的工程图。

最后还能直接连到 3D 打印、钣金和 CNC 加工服务，下单，把实物做出来。

Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Gemini 都能装。从一句话到一个拿在手里的零件，中间不需要你会建模。

10 OpenSRE

https://t.co/Sa4sLCsKYs

最后一个，OpenSRE，让 AI 帮你值夜班。

一万一千九百颗星，一月份建库，现在还是公开测试版。

SRE 就是负责线上服务稳定的工程师。半夜服务出了问题，证据散在日志、监控指标、调用链路、最近的发布记录，还有一堆聊天消息里，得一个个去翻。

OpenSRE 是一套开源工具，让你搭自己的 AI SRE。告警一来，它自动去拉相关的日志、指标、链路和最近的部署，先把敏感的标识打上码，再交给模型。

模型在你接好的六十多种工具之间来回查，提出假设、验证假设，最后给你一个带证据的结论，建议怎么修，你同意的话还能直接动手修，再把总结发到 Slack。

你也可以在命令行里直接问它：为什么结账接口变慢了？

他们想做的，是 AI 运维的训练场：把成千上万种真实的线上故障做成测试，让 AI 在里面练。

Ali Ghodsi of @Databricks on the four conditions that would have to hold for AI to truly improve itself:

"The next model requires less resources, less GPUs to train... The second condition: the next model takes less time to train as well. Third, accuracy of the model, the intelligence is increasing. And fourth, we can do the former three again and again and again... All at the same time, not just any of them."

"If you just mean that the software is writing itself, we're already there today. Like 90-some percent of the software in Databricks is written by AI. Does it matter if the last few percent is also written by AI? No."

"If you're getting these four conditions, then you might get a speed-up where the next model, let's say, takes half amount of time and half the resources, and it is more intelligent... By the way, I don't even know if that necessarily leads you to superintelligence."

"A lot of people, their definition is just, 'Hey, if I'm not even coding anymore and it's coding itself'... I think they're conflating, 'Hey, what's my value and is it scary for me?' Versus, 'Hey, that then means we'll get that superintelligence that in 2014 was hypothesized by Bostrom.'"

author: siddsanyal
quoted_text:
When I was writing Unreal Engine 1, my time was divided as follows:

- Around 30% went to seriously deep coding on hard problems: assembly language texture mappers, C++ BSP trees, data persistence, object oriented systems design, and networking.

- Around 70% was just typing and refactoring large bodies of code needed for a complete engine feature set. This was not hard, and while I was doing it my mind was mostly on the deeper coding topics, thinking and planning for what's next. It didn't feel much different from vibe coding today, except that it was just me typing code on an IBM Model M keyboard rather than prompting it and reviewing the results.

So, it has always seemed perfectly logical that we would rely on AI for that 70%, once the AI could do it with a similar quality standard as we could, which has never been perfection. It came as no surprise that, after a few years of AI model evolution, it was able to take the reigns on that 70% and free up programmers' time for more valuable tasks.

What's more of a surprise is the emergence of AI as a sort of insta-Carmack able to solve hard technical problems quite cleverly and often cleanly, and that it's able to reason about and work in complex 3D scenes both by operating the tools and by directly understanding the raw data files.

I abandoned assembly language in 1998 when out-of-order CPUs made much simpler C/C++ code faster, and never I missed it. If prompting through architectural documents, concept art, and design plans can transcend typing code and tweaking vertices, that will enable developers to spend their time on higher-level, higher value technical and creative tasks.

What matters is the end product, whether it's a game or an engine. Anything developers can do to try out more ideas and make better software and games faster is a win for everyone.

quoted_text:
The recent trajectory of $DOPE looks quite similar to $FARTCOIN.

33jENUQnjoitkMFpvNJcSHyLAHFWJuHwT6E3E8CNpump 

Both are built around absurd stories created by AI, which spread across the internet before someone launched a token around them, turning attention that was previously impossible to price into a tradable asset.

That is the common ground between Fartcoin and DOPE.

Fartcoin didn’t begin as a traditional startup project. The story that attracted the most attention was connected to the AI agent Truth Terminal. An absurd narrative built around AI, internet humor, and fart jokes gradually escaped its original context and became a meme in its own right. Fartcoin then brought that cultural expression into the crypto market.

It didn’t need to prove that it had sophisticated technology or rely on a mature product to justify its existence. The name was straightforward, the joke was easy to understand, and the barrier to sharing it was low. Even someone who knew nothing about AI agents could get the joke.

This doesn’t mean AI alone was responsible for Fartcoin’s success. But it demonstrated a possibility: an absurd idea that initially appeared to have no value could still attract enormous attention at the intersection of internet culture and crypto.

DOPE’s story came from a different direction. Someone was trying to create a 3D Doge Pepe image when they accidentally consumed more than 400 million tokens, generating an AI usage bill of around $1,900. What began as an expensive mistake became a story that people could easily share because of the staggering number, the absurdity of the incident, and the instantly recognizable Doge Pepe image.

The most interesting part is that AI was supposed to improve efficiency and reduce the cost of creation. Instead, an unexpected mistake produced a joke that was far easier for people to remember.

Meme culture is particularly good at exploiting this kind of contrast. The technology becomes more advanced, yet the experience becomes more ridiculous. People expect AI to make things more efficient, only to end up with an expensive image and a story that can be shared over and over again. The humor requires no complicated explanation.

This is where DOPE’s narrative connects with Fartcoin. They are not the same story, nor did they emerge through exactly the same mechanism. But both demonstrate that AI doesn’t have to enter the crypto market through products, technological breakthroughs, or commercial success. It can also become meme material through an unexpected incident, an absurd piece of content, or even a joke that initially seems too trivial to take seriously.

A story becoming a meme doesn’t necessarily mean it can sustain a token. And a token going up in the short term doesn’t mean it has established lasting cultural relevance.

There is an important conversion process in between. First, people need to remember the story. Then they need to repeat it, imitate it, and create their own variations. As the story spreads, more people begin to develop a shared understanding of the symbol. Once a token enters the picture, people also gain a way to trade and speculate on that story.

This is one of the differences between a meme coin and an ordinary internet trend. Attention around a normal trend can simply disappear, while a token converts some of that attention into price, holdings, and trading activity. When the market believes a story still has room to spread, buying the token means betting not only on its name but also on its potential to attract future attention.

Early exposure may come from the story itself. Subsequent price appreciation, however, increasingly depends on new buyers, liquidity, and market expectations. Once the story loses its novelty, or the community can no longer produce new content around it, its original narrative advantage can fade quickly.

DOPE is following a path that has appeared in the market before. That does not mean it will end up in the same place as Fartcoin.

What matters is that Fartcoin has already demonstrated that an absurd, accessible AI-related narrative can become the starting point for a major meme coin. DOPE now faces a different question: can a story born from an AI usage mishap evolve beyond its initial newsworthiness and become a symbol that people continue to spread? Will more people actively participate in creating, sharing, and trading around it? And once the initial excitement fades, will it still have the ability to attract attention?

For DOPE, the real test isn’t whether its story can make people laugh once. It’s whether people will still want to tell that story after the laughter fades.

At the moment, holding DOPE also gives holders exposure to ANTHROPIC, DOGE, and PEPE. That makes the direction particularly interesting. Let’s keep watching how it develops.

quoted_text:
The $DOPE team has taken the original DOPE meme narrative a step further by turning it into a product: a meme-style asset basket that automatically rewards holders with multiple tokens.

33jENUQnjoitkMFpvNJcSHyLAHFWJuHwT6E3E8CNpump 

If DOPE initially gained attention from the AI accident that cost nearly $1,900 and produced just one Doge × Pepe image, the website is now taking that story one step further.

Holders of DOPE automatically receive three reward tokens: ANTHROPIC, DOGE, and PEPE, with no manual claiming required. The project describes this mechanism as “RWA-style rewards” for memes. It is not an RWA in the traditional sense of being backed by real-world assets, but rather a product concept borrowed from the idea of holding one asset and automatically receiving a basket of related assets.

What makes this design interesting is that DOPE is no longer just a hybrid meme character. It now has an additional economic narrative that can continue to spread.

Doge and Pepe represent the two cultural sources of the character, while ANTHROPIC connects it to the original AI API incident. Together, the three names form an easy-to-understand combination: hold a meme accidentally created by AI, and receive tokens associated with its story and origins.

This adds another layer to the narrative beyond simply repeating the story of spending $1,900 to generate one image. The original incident attracts attention, the hybrid character provides recognition, and the reward mechanism attempts to give people an ongoing reason to hold.

From a product perspective, the idea is to encourage users to do more than simply buy and wait for the price to rise. Instead, they receive reward tokens while holding. Automatic distribution with no claiming required also lowers the barrier to participation.

However, it is important to distinguish the design presented on the project’s website from economic value that has actually been verified.

The website displays approximately 549 SOL in reward value and around 125,900 payouts. However, it explicitly labels these figures as an approximate baseline used while the OTC data feed is unreachable, rather than a verified live snapshot. Rewards are distributed in tokens, not directly in SOL. Therefore, these figures cannot be treated as verified cash payouts worth 549 SOL, nor can the actual value of the rewards be determined solely from the number of distributions.

More importantly, the names of the reward tokens and their connection to the narrative do not mean they have stable value. To determine whether this mechanism genuinely strengthens DOPE’s fundamentals, we still need to verify where the rewards come from, how they are distributed, whether distributions continue consistently, and whether the reward tokens have actual market liquidity.

I think the most important question is whether this mechanism can turn one-time narrative-driven attention into a more lasting reason to hold.

If the rewards continue, the rules remain transparent, and the community genuinely creates new content around these three tokens, DOPE could evolve from a meme born out of an AI accident into a meme project with a story, a recognizable character, and a holding mechanism.

But if the rewards are merely short-term marketing, or if their actual value falls significantly short of what the website suggests, the mechanism may simply add another layer of packaging to the existing narrative rather than create a genuinely sustainable economic cycle.

For that reason, I see this update as an attempt to turn DOPE’s narrative into a product, rather than proof that its value-capture mechanism has been validated. The next things worth verifying are the on-chain reward distributions, the source of the rewards, actual liquidity, and whether the mechanism continues operating after the initial speculative hype fades.

DOPE initially gained recognition through an absurd AI story. Now it is trying to give holders another reason to stay through an automatic reward mechanism. A compelling story can get someone to buy for the first time; sustained content creation and a credible reward mechanism are what might convince them to stay.

quoted_text:
$CLAUDIA is worth paying attention to because it may be more than just a Meme that has attracted Elon's attention.

2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

It could be an early experiment in a new AI-powered IP incubation model, and $HeavyPulp is a valuable case study to reference.

Anabology has already received comments and replies from Elon Musk multiple times. Five interactions in a row suggest that Claudia-related content has not simply appeared on his radar by chance, but has demonstrated an ability to repeatedly capture his attention. That matters.

For most Memes, the hardest part is not launching a token, but finding a source of attention that can be activated repeatedly. Many projects have to keep chasing new trends, riding one person's popularity today and another event tomorrow. Once the external narrative disappears, the community often struggles to keep producing content.

CLAUDIA's potential advantage is that it has an ongoing creative force behind it.

Anabology is not just managing a token. He is trying to use AI to build a virtual character IP that can continue to evolve. This leads me to a more ambitious idea: Could we eventually see a model in which AI autonomously produces high-quality short dramas, continuously creates content around a recurring character, and then uses a token to fund further production?

The short dramas create content, the content attracts attention, the attention flows into the token market, and the fees generated by trading are then used to fund the next round of production. As long as the quality remains high enough, this mechanism could form a positive feedback loop.

The difference from traditional Memes is that the token would no longer be just a symbol waiting to be speculated on. It could become a financing and incentive tool within the content production process.

Of course, this model still needs to be validated in practice, but the potential is clear: if AI can continually lower the cost of producing high-quality content, an IP could generate attention more frequently without relying entirely on the production cycles of the traditional film and television industry.

Claudia provides a useful opportunity to explore this direction.

Elon's repeated interactions are an important attention catalyst in this model. Elon has an enormous reach, and when he repeatedly engages with a creator's work, that content can break out of its original audience. More importantly, when these interactions happen repeatedly, the market starts paying attention to the creator's next release and whether another repost or reply might follow.

This gives Claudia an ongoing series of potential catalysts rather than just a one-time news event.

That is why I believe HeavyPulp is a valuable case study. It demonstrates one possible path: a creator attracts Elon's attention through AI-generated content, a token narrative forms around the creator and their work, and the token is then connected to future content production.

If CLAUDIA can develop along the same path, with Anabology continuously producing content, Elon's interactions amplifying its exposure, and the token mechanism providing funding for further creation, every new release could become another catalyst.

This is why I am paying attention to Anabology's content output. Rather than simply waiting for Elon to reply again, I want to see whether Claudia can continue producing high-quality short videos, establish a recognizable character identity, and gradually attract more creators to participate.

Once Claudia is no longer just Anabology's personal creation but becomes an IP that the community actively wants to expand, its narrative ceiling could rise significantly.

For CLAUDIA, the most promising scenario is not that Elon replies once more and the token rallies again. It is that AI content continues to be produced, Elon's attention amplifies its reach, and the token funds further creation, ultimately forming an attention cycle that can be activated repeatedly.

If this experiment succeeds, CLAUDIA could become more than a Meme dependent on celebrity interactions. It could represent an early attempt at an AI-native content economy.

text:
I have always believed that one fundamental reason so many $ELON tokens in the past failed to gain real traction was that they had nothing more than Elon's name.

B2GESkSErPjuCq6n4LcaJP5v2z1kJnw3xHVZnop2sZx 

They never established an economic connection to the ecosystem associated with Elon.

When you bought them, you were buying a Meme and betting on Elon’s influence, but Elon’s ability to continuously create companies, products, and new narratives would not automatically translate into value for those tokens.

This is why I believe this ELON is worth examining again.

What I care about is not simply that it combines Meme, stocks, and RWA, but that StonkFun is attempting to connect these elements into a mechanism that can actually operate.

ELON’s liquidity pool is paired with MUSK4, which is described as a basket of tokenized assets related to Elon, including TSLA, SPCX, Neuralink, and DOGE.

The idea is not to bet on Tesla alone, but to bet on Elon himself and his ability to continuously create companies, assets, and new narratives. Memes provide the means of spreading, Elon provides global attention, RWA provides the real-asset narrative, and MUSK4 attempts to condense this entire Elon ecosystem into a single asset basket.

More importantly, StonkFun is attempting to make holding ELON about more than simply waiting for the next hype cycle. According to the mechanism displayed on the platform, every ELON transfer incurs a 1% tax, which is distributed proportionally to holders in MUSK4. When the platform holds a relatively large share of the ELON supply, some rounds also distribute ELON itself.

If this mechanism can operate sustainably, holding ELON is no longer just a bet on Elon’s attention. Holders may also obtain related asset tokens through the reward mechanism. In the past, “BUY ELON” was just a Meme slogan. Now, it is beginning to take on a more concrete economic meaning.

Of course, I would not equate holding ELON with directly owning equity in TSLA, SPCX, or Neuralink. MUSK4’s specific asset composition, underlying backing, liquidity, and the actual rights enjoyed by its holders all need to be independently verified. But I believe a meaningful change is worth paying attention to: ELON is attempting to evolve from a Meme that simply borrows Elon’s name into a trading vehicle that connects the Elon narrative, a basket of related assets, and economic incentives for holders.

The StonkFun data from the past 14 hours is an important basis for my judgment that this mechanism is becoming more active. The number of holders increased from 2,779 to 4,144, an increase of 1,365, or approximately 49.1%. The cumulative amount of MUSK4 distributed increased from 35.72K to 75.33K, a rise of approximately 110.9%. The cumulative number of distribution payments increased from 31,769 to 60,169, a rise of approximately 89.4%. Meanwhile, the current dollar value of cumulative MUSK4 distributions increased from $35,846 to $74,479.

I pay more attention to these metrics changing simultaneously than to how much the price has risen on its own. The holder base is expanding, the scale of reward distributions is increasing, and the distribution records continue to accumulate. Together, these indicate that market participation and mechanism activity are strengthening at the same time. They do not prove that all newly added addresses are long-term users, nor can the entire cumulative increase be attributed directly to these 14 hours. But they at least show that this mechanism is leaving a record of continued operation rather than remaining merely a concept.

There are also two details on the rewards page worth paying attention to. The pending MUSK4 queue declined from approximately 1.67K, valued at $1,671 at current prices, to 96.62 MUSK4, valued at $95.53. At the same time, pending tax fees increased from $76.95 to $1,740. This indicates that between the two snapshots, the pending MUSK4 queue decreased significantly while new tax fees continued to accumulate, potentially entering the distribution process later. If trading activity remains strong, this provides a metric we can track to assess the continued operation of the reward mechanism.

Distributions in ELON itself are also continuing. The cumulative amount distributed increased from 31.63M to 31.66M, while the number of distribution payments increased from 1,435 to 1,440. One point needs to be noted here: the actual token amount increased by only around 30,000, or approximately 0.095%, while its corresponding dollar value rose from $51,408 to $63,721. Therefore, I would not attribute the entire increase in dollar value to growth in the amount distributed. What matters more is that the page shows this distribution mechanism continuing to operate, rather than an apparent improvement in fundamentals created simply by rising prices.

Changes in holder positions are also worth tracking. The top wallet held 34.42M ELON in both screenshots, accounting for approximately 3.44% of the supply, but the estimated value of its holdings increased from $50,480 to $70,296. This reflects the impact of price changes on the valuation of its holdings, rather than the wallet accumulating more tokens. The second-largest wallet increased from 33.48M to 34.21M, the third-largest increased from 28.81M to 29.10M, and the fourth remained at 26.72M. Several other large wallets also showed increases: the wallet beginning with 3r7E increased from 20.82M to 21.74M, the wallet beginning with GZet increased from 18.85M to 20.93M, and the wallet beginning with mDR9 increased from 16.30M to 20.25M. Meanwhile, the wallet beginning with AYZr decreased from 21.97M to 19.43M, while the wallet beginning with BmPY remained at 17.06M.

So I would not interpret this as a situation in which all large holders are accumulating in unison, but the data currently visible also does not show a broad decline in top-holder positions. The rapid expansion in the holder base, alongside increases in the holdings of some large wallets, is at least a signal worth continuing to monitor. We still need to examine the actual capital represented by new addresses, related wallets, and net buying and selling to determine whether this expansion can continue.

Another change is that ELON has appeared in StonkFun’s active Ecosystem Flywheel rankings. The page records 20 buybacks, with a cumulative buyback-and-burn amount of $32.08. This amount is still very small, and I would not exaggerate it into buying pressure capable of supporting the valuation. But it gives us a new dimension to monitor: whether revenue from the platform ecosystem can gradually translate into additional demand for ELON through actual buybacks and burns. Being included in the flywheel rankings does not mean the platform has committed to conducting buybacks in the future. What is worth watching next is whether buybacks continue to occur, whether their amounts increase, and whether they eventually become meaningful relative to the token’s circulating market capitalization.

Putting these changes together, I believe ELON’s fundamentals have strengthened at the margin over the past 14 hours. The most significant improvements are in holder growth and reward mechanism activity, while buybacks and burns have also produced preliminary execution records. However, I would not describe this as a mature value flywheel that has already been established, because genuine user retention, MUSK4’s asset-related rights, and the extent to which platform revenue can generate meaningful buying demand for ELON have not yet been sufficiently verified.

Looking ahead, I care most about three potential drivers of further upside. First, whether the number of holders can continue to grow, and whether new addresses can gradually turn into participants with actual purchasing power. If trading activity and net buying expand together, ELON could move beyond being a short-lived trend driven by a small group of traders and develop into a market asset with broader participation.

Second, whether MUSK4’s asset composition, underlying backing, and holder rights can be verified more transparently. If the asset basket has clear, verifiable economic exposure, the market’s understanding of ELON could expand from that of a Meme borrowing Elon’s name to that of a trading vehicle built around the narrative of Elon-related assets.

Third, and most importantly, whether StonkFun’s revenue can gradually translate into meaningful ELON buybacks and burns. If trading activity expands, rewards continue to be distributed, and buybacks and burns keep growing, this mechanism may have a chance to form a genuine positive feedback loop: trading demand generates more economic activity, the reward mechanism provides additional incentives to hold, and platform revenue creates additional demand for the token through buybacks and burns.

Beyond these factors, new developments involving Elon-related companies, AI and space narratives, as well as another wave of attention generated by Elon himself, could all serve as external catalysts for further upside. But I do not want to build the investment thesis around whether Elon will post again. Celebrity attention can accelerate a rally, but it should not be the only source of growth for this token.

This is why I am bullish on ELON: it is attempting to solve a longstanding problem with traditional Elon Memes by connecting the attention surrounding Elon with economic incentives that holders may actually receive. Meme gives it the ability to spread, Elon gives it a global narrative entry point, MUSK4 gives it the potential of an asset basket, and StonkFun’s reward and buyback mechanisms attempt to add a layer of economic activity that can be continuously verified.

This mechanism is still at an early stage, and the buyback amount remains very small. But the expansion in holders, reward distributions, and preliminary buybacks already provide changes worth monitoring. If asset transparency, reward delivery, and effective value capture are all validated over time, the reason for the market to reassess ELON will no longer need to come solely from what Elon says next. It could instead come from how large this trading and asset mechanism associated with Elon can ultimately become.

For me, this is the long-term direction of ELON that is most worth betting on.

text:
Perplexity 宣布将开源逆向工程工具 REA（Reverse Engineer Anything）接入 Computer。用户只需告诉 AI 想复刻哪款软件，它就能在没有原始源代码的情况下，分析软件的运行方式，再尝试重新编写一个功能相似的版本。

Perplexity 一口气展示了 5 款复刻作品，全部提供可在线体验的网页版本：

1. Figma：支持图层、自动布局、多人实时协作，以及账号登录和跨设备同步。
2. LibreOffice Calc：支持编辑单元格、编写公式，修改数据后图表自动更新。
3. Photopea：类似网页版 Photoshop，支持图层、蒙版、调色和文字编辑。
4. Harvey：面向法律工作的 AI 工具，可以搜索合同、比较不同版本，并根据指定规则标记条款，附上原文引用。
5. Audacity：支持音频剪辑、混音、音量调整、淡入淡出，以及导出 WAV 文件。

REA 由开发者 morluto 开源，能够配合 Ghidra、Hopper 等工具，分析程序内部的函数、调用关系和运行行为，也能检查网页及 JavaScript、Electron 应用。不过，这并不意味着 AI 已经能完整复制商业软件。REA 作者明确表示，工具无法保证还原原始源码。

Perplexity 为这项功能提供限时免费额度。10 月 31 日前，使用 `/reverse-engineer` 的任务可享受每人最多 10,000 Credits 的免费额度。

“What I’ve learned is that it’s not really some arbitrary management tactics, but it’s really used as a rigorous engineering and first principle, you know. Again, this is more applicable in the world of atoms, but we have this concept called all green light schedule, which is kind of forcing us to think about if every single light is green, there’s no administrative burdens or delays or no shipping delays or risk or no legacy bottlenecks, how fast can you build it?”

“And when you think from that point of view and vantage point and literally strip away any man-made bottlenecks and you ask a question of how fast can you actually manufacture a chip, how fast can you design a robot and test it. Ben Horowitz: “The most dangerous thing going on in AI is Anthropic and Bill Gates”

“Anybody can go say, ‘AI is going to kill us,’ and you'll be on every major news station and every newspaper and so forth.

I think it's extremely dangerous, though, when it comes from Bill Gates because he is so credible, because he did build Microsoft, and people think of him that way, and then certainly he's been a big political donor, so he has a lot of political juice, particularly on the Democratic side.

The big risk that everybody talks about is that the models are going to recursively self-improve, and then they're going to take off, and then they're going to become so smart and run away from us.

Well, what would be the preconditions for that?

Ali Ghodsi from Databricks had a great formulation of, ‘Well, what would be the preconditions for that?’

And he had four preconditions.

One is that the next model has to require fewer GPUs than the last.

The second thing is the next model has to take less time to train.

And then the accuracy of the next model has to be better than the last, so it's got to be a better model.

And then finally, it's gotta keep happening again and again and again.

Zero of those four have been met.

We're not on track for any of those four to be met, and so we're really talking about a risk that's entirely theoretical at this point that we're not mapping to.”

text:
Every time you think Apple is about to give up on Vision Pro, it comes out with something that reminds you why the platform is worth paying attention to.

The newly released immersive horror short Remnants is genuinely impressive. I highly recommend it to every Vision Pro user.

A few things really stood out to me.

1. The 3D and sense of presence. The film recreates a 19th-century European castle in incredible detail, from its grand architecture and interior layout to the furniture, paintings, and decorations. The 3D looks fantastic. Actually feeling like you’re inside the castle, looking around and taking in the space, is something traditional 2D cinema simply can’t replicate.

2. The atmosphere. The rain, dim lighting, and spatial audio work beautifully together. The horror isn’t just about jump scares. It’s the entire environment that creates this constant sense of unease and tension.

3. The filmmaking. At 27 minutes, I think the length is just right. Any longer and it might actually be too much horror for me. Director Ti West is an established Hollywood horror filmmaker, best known for X and Pearl. Just like Submerged, Apple has brought in an experienced filmmaker with a strong command of cinematic storytelling to explore what’s possible with Immersive Video.

Of course, immersive filmmaking is still far from perfect. Some cuts feel abrupt, and traditional editing techniques don’t always translate naturally to a 180° immersive environment.

But after watching this, I’m more convinced than ever of one thing.

Immersive Video has the potential to deliver cinematic experiences that are fundamentally better than traditional flat-screen movies.

The question is no longer whether the medium has potential. It’s that filmmakers are still figuring out its own unique cinematic language.

Give it time. The potential here is enormous.

Q1: How do we explain last week’s crypto volatility?
A1: Leverage flush, not capitulation.

-BTC fell from $87K to $80K with $1B+ liquidated.
-Oil, Hormuz and rate fears drove institutions to de-risk, pulling $1.2B from BTC and ETH ETFs.
-The flush was far smaller than last year’s $19B (AED 70B) day, so venues absorbed it cleanly.

Q2: What does the market need to recover?

A2: Oil and yields to ease.
-US CPI on Oct 14 and the Fed on Oct 28 are the key tests.
-ETF flows turning positive again, led by institutions.
-Leverage is already reset.

text:
I think the biggest beneficiary of America's war on immigration might be the Indian startup ecosystem. The American Dream was always rented and never been a better time than now for Indian engineers to build at home. India isn’t the India of the 90s when engineers moved out for better pay and exposure. Earlier generations left India because they didn’t have a choice but today, staying back is the smarter choice. 

Just need a few thousands of our engineers to become founders. Sure, we have our own constraints and we still have infrastructure gaps and bureaucracy is still frustrating. But if you look back at history, Indian engineers have always thrived precisely in moments of constraint.

The outsourcing opportunity of the 90s was born from labour cost arbitrage. The SaaS opportunity of the 2010s came from building global software with frugal & distributed teams. The next cycle will be no different. 

This is the great inversion of our time and for the first time in history, the opportunity cost of leaving India may be greater than the opportunity cost of staying.Time to build for India and from India.

@bhorowitz point is that scaling compute on debt is a dangerous arbitrage business, and he lived it in 99 when bandwidth was $1,500/megabit and the only way to get it was a 3 year contract. By 2001 it was $50 - If you were holding that on borrowed money you were dead.

His case for $CRWV being different is that AI compute is in a massive shortage, so GPU and data center prices keep rising. Maybe he's right. But the neocloud model is still a levered bet that GPU scarcity outlasts the debt, because they borrow against the GPUs and the lenders get paid on a schedule whether or not the market cooperates. 

A compute subnet on Bittensor is basically a decentralized neocloud that doesn't need any of that. There's no GPU purchase to finance (miners show up with their own hardware) and no 3 year capacity contract to get stuck holding if prices move. The token + the network do the job the debt does for CoreWeave. Emissions bootstrap the supply side, and as demand and revenue grow the subnet puts that value back into its token, which raises what miners earn and pulls more compute onto the network. The token is the lever that scales how much compute you can harvest and coordinate. So if GPU pricing ever pulls a Loudcloud, the subnet doesn't blow up, its incentives just buy more compute than they used to.

With no debt there's nothing to default on, and nobody can call a loan or force a fire sale. The risk you take on instead is token volatility, which you manage with a treasury (keep cash on hand and use it to support your token through drawdowns). A bad market can starve a subnet for a while, but one with real demand underneath it can ride that out.

The tradeoff is a slower, more gradual build. A neocloud can borrow its way to a giant cluster fast, while a subnet's capacity grows with the size of the network and the token. What you get in exchange is a far more durable business, mostly because of where the supply comes from. You're tapping a bunch of long tails of compute that a neocloud can't really get at:

>people who own their own hardware and want to monetize it when they're not using it
>slack capacity in data centers (nobody runs at 100%), which can get sold into the subnet's spot market instead of sitting idle
>sunk cost hardware, i.e. paid off GPUs that can't get a contract for anything else
>operators in places with cheap power that no lender would ever underwrite a data center for

Once a card is paid off the main ongoing cost is power, which even on an H100 is something like 5-10 cents an hour depending on where you are. So a lot of this supply is pretty price insensitive. They make more when the token is higher, but a 50% drawdown in miner rewards eats into their margin and plenty of them keep mining anyway. That gives you a structural supply floor that doesn't really care what the token (and therefore the miner reward) is doing day to day.

Then as network value and the token go up, you progressively unlock compute that's more price sensitive (financed GPUs that still have to pay themselves off, US data centers with pricier power, etc). Each one joins once mining becomes economic for it, and you get a flywheel: token up → more of the world's compute profitable to plug in → more capacity to sell → more revenue → more value back into the token → repeat. Every GPU that joins also makes the network cheaper and more reliable to buy from, so you get a real network effect on top of removing the debt risk.

And in the limit it can reach more compute than any single hyperscaler could ever build or finance, because the supply side is permissionless and global. You start by tapping into the world's edge compute, and over time the rest of the world's compute comes online as it makes economic sense for whoever owns it.

text:
When I was writing Unreal Engine 1, my time was divided as follows:

- Around 30% went to seriously deep coding on hard problems: assembly language texture mappers, C++ BSP trees, data persistence, object oriented systems design, and networking.

- Around 70% was just typing and refactoring large bodies of code needed for a complete engine feature set. This was not hard, and while I was doing it my mind was mostly on the deeper coding topics, thinking and planning for what's next. It didn't feel much different from vibe coding today, except that it was just me typing code on an IBM Model M keyboard rather than prompting it and reviewing the results.

So, it has always seemed perfectly logical that we would rely on AI for that 70%, once the AI could do it with a similar quality standard as we could, which has never been perfection. It came as no surprise that, after a few years of AI model evolution, it was able to take the reigns on that 70% and free up programmers' time for more valuable tasks.

What's more of a surprise is the emergence of AI as a sort of insta-Carmack able to solve hard technical problems quite cleverly and often cleanly, and that it's able to reason about and work in complex 3D scenes both by operating the tools and by directly understanding the raw data files.

I abandoned assembly language in 1998 when out-of-order CPUs made much simpler C/C++ code faster, and never I missed it. If prompting through architectural documents, concept art, and design plans can transcend typing code and tweaking vertices, that will enable developers to spend their time on higher-level, higher value technical and creative tasks.

What matters is the end product, whether it's a game or an engine. Anything developers can do to try out more ideas and make better software and games faster is a win for everyone.
