text:
Contrarian Thinking.

Over and over the contrarians are the ones who change the world. But it is a muscle that needs constant exercise. The masses have the market share and most people hate change.

"I would never share my house with others." AirBnb was born.

"I would never use a digital camera," I heard at Eastman Kodak's booth years ago. Today I shoot all my photos on iPhone.

"I love to drive." Today I often take a Waymo.

"Babies use mice and GUIs." I heard that one in college from a Unix programmer. Now we are headed into a world where we don't use mice and GUIs, thanks to voice systems and brain computer interface companies.

"Art can't be done with AI." Now when you are the Sphere in Las Vegas you are watching a movie dramatically improved with AI.

"Our customers love buttons," engineers at Mercedes Benz said, while pointing out to me that touching screens is more dangerous while driving than touching buttons.

"Cooking with microwaves isn't as good as using an open flame," many chefs have told me. Yet when you arrive home late and need to make something for the kids do you listen to the chefs?

"I'll never use a phone without a physical keyboard," many told me. Yet here we are.

"I'll never use an autofocus camera," many pro photographers told me. Now it is weird if you see a pro manually focusing. 

So, how can you build your contrarian muscle?

Go back to the core problem that humans are trying to solve and rethink it without bias. 

On Friday @broodsugar told the audience at @TheHumanoidHub's event that a Chinese retailer asked themselves "what if humans actually suck at running a retailer." They automated every decision. AI manages every store. Makes every decision of where to put products, and how many to stock, that kind of thing. Sales went up 258%. And this was a well established retailer with billions in sales every year. 

Other ways I was able to get ahead of everyone when I wrote my eight books (I wrote a book about social media before Twitter started). 

1. Learn about bleeding edge tech and ask yourself "what if this got adopted?"

2. Hang around with others who have demonstrated contrarian thinking. 

3. Dream about what the world would look like if your new thing actually worked for everyone. Would the world improve or get worse?

4. Learn some secrets that very few others know. I once talked at Google's first advertiser's conference and they sat me at a VIP table with Kraft food execs. They told me why they advertise and told me how much they spend to acquire a new customer. $34. So when Instagram was bought by Mark Zuckerberg I knew it was an amazing purchase, since Instagram's users were growing exponentially every few weeks. I gave a speech to billionaires that morning who thought it was the stupidest purchase they ever had heard of. It had no sales. No profits. 14 employees. No assets. That is consensus thinking. Which they got into because that's how businesses were (and still are) measured. 

5. Study the problems that people actually are having and then find new ways to solve those problems with fresh eyes. Heck, you can see this in action by visiting @reservoirfarms, that has 20 new companies building farming robots. Every entrepreneur I talked with there spent years walking in farms with farmers, understanding their problems, before they started building robots. I have met many entrepreneurs who worked in weird jobs to learn the industry they are going after. Have you worked on a manufacturing line? In a dentist's office? Or, done landscaping? "First principles" applies to every human endeavor.

6. Learn from Eric Reis. When he was building one of his first companies he spent months building software that he thought people would want. When he launched it no one visited his home page. He learned to test his weird ideas first before he built another thing. 

7. Hang out with people who are different. Years ago I got to hang out with Steve Mann. I shot this photo in 2014, and he had already worn a device on his face for 20 years, even had a screw implanted in his skull so that he could more easily wear a wearable computer. He was weird, let's be honest. Never met someone like him before. But ask yourself "what if he is right, and everyone else is wrong?" There are armies who will tell you they never will wear smart glasses, even today. Can you resist armies who will give you every reason why they never will do the new weird thing?

8. Hang out with the young. I remember being in Hyde Jr. High's first computer club in Cupertino back in 1977. Only five people in it. There were armies of older people (and even many other kids) who would tell me they never would use one and had no need for it. I hung out with @photomatt in San Francisco 20 years ago when he was only 17, and hearing his dreams of how people and companies would publish in the future radically changed my life for the past 20 years. Same for interviewing @VitalikButerin when he was about that age. Laid out an entirely new economics system based on smart contracts. Mullenweg had just started his company and saw a new way for humans to communicate. Today, what, 80% of the Web is running on his software, Wordpress. As much as I hate it, it is rare that people my age (I'm now almost 62) comes up with such a radical shift. It does happen, but far more likely that a 17 year old is gonna build a dramatically important company than I am. Why? They are not burdened by "the way things are done."

9. Ask yourself "is there a better way to do this?" Steve Jobs told his original iPhone team not to hire anyone who worked on a phone at any other company. He didn't want to hear why something wouldn't work, he wanted fresh thinking and new ideas. Back to getting rid of buttons.

10. Question your own assumptions. They might be completely wrong. Mine often are. And be OK with that. I once said that I would wear a Google Glass the rest of my life. That was wrong, obviously. Sometimes I talk myself into points of view that don't turn out to be right. At least short term. (I still am looking for a pair that will make that a right statement). 

11. Build and test with humans who won't blow smoke up your ass (not your friends and family). 

12. Read a lot of books. Anyone who writes a book has thought a LOT about what they are presenting. They often see cracks in consensus thinking. Yeah, often they are science fiction authors, but often not. (I have to take that advice more myself, dropped off my reading). Especially true regarding people who write about new ideas and how to put them into use in business (same here on X, which is why if I find a contrarian thinker I put them on my lists).

13. Remember "experts" are people who got good at building for the masses. But they often have deep blind spots on where the future will be and they often will give you bad advice. 

14. Ask yourself "what if everyone had an autonomous car, a VR headset, a robot, a brain computer interface?" What would be needed that doesn't exist in such a world? 

15. Question your world view. I once was highly religious, went to church three times on Sunday. Thought I was right back then too. And religion is still the dominant world view most people have, but it isn't the only one. Ask most people about autonomous cars and you'll hear religion come back "I'll never let the government look at me while I drive." That's a belief system that person is locked into. 

16. Ask yourself "how could I change even the worst hater?" One "secret" I learned over and over in my career is people change, and even give up religious belief systems, when presented with something new. Henry Ford used to say "if I asked people what they wanted, they answered 'a better horse.'" They couldn't dream of a contraption that would drive them around. Even last night I talked with a Stanford Fellow who gave me the same answer about autonomous cars. He used to run California Microwave, is a very smart guy, but used to have a race car and is stuck in the world view of "I love to drive." 

I could go for quite a while longer, but wanted to open it up to you. 

How do you put contrarian thinking into use in your own life/business or in the things you are building? Are you starting a contarian company? One that, if successful, will force everyone to change? 

This post due to Brendan Footy, @BrendanFoody cofounder of Mercor, who shared this post this morning: https://t.co/jcDgICpl4m

text:
I've been critical in the past of AI compute indexes and the willingness to price compute based on the spot rental price, but now that the AI reset is sinking into the repricing of AI buildout debt its time to realize that the cost of capital is what determines the price of compute.

The most important number in GPU pricing right now isn't $/GPU-hour. It's the gap between what a hyperscaler pays to borrow (~90bp over Treasuries) and what a neocloud pays (~1,100bp).

The cost of compute is now set by the cost of capital, and the spot rental rate no longer tells you much.
 The price of an H100 isn't one number. The same chip in the same rack costs a different amount depending on whose balance sheet it sits on. A ~1,000bp funding gap is a structural cost advantage that no amount of operating skill closes.

For example, take one GPU-hour apart. Most of it isn't power or space. It's paying back the chip, the interest on the loan that bought it, and the return the equity expects. A $40–55k all-in GPU, 75% debt-funded, at ~7,000 utilized hours a year is a financing instrument that happens to do matrix multiplication.
As the +500bp on neocloud debt (10%→15%) adds $0.20–0.30 to the break-even cost of every GPU-hour, which is then added on to the rental price.
That's 8–10% of the H100 index, from a credit spread alone, driven almost entirely by the cost of capital.

That means that the compute spot index is a derivative of the AI infra debt credit curve and the squeeze on neocloud margins.

text:
Delete your CLAUDE.md. Not edit it, not trim it, delete the whole file, along with your skills and your hooks, and see what the model does without them. That's Boris Cherny's actual advice from a recent YC appearance, and the Claude Code team has apparently followed it internally enough times that roughly 80% of their own system prompts are gone. His reasoning: most of those rules patched a weakness in whatever model you ran six or twelve months ago. Newer models often don't have that weakness anymore, so the instruction that used to help is now just constraining a more capable model for no reason. His method is almost embarrassingly plain. Delete everything, work normally for a while, watch where the model actually goes off track, add back exactly one instruction when a mistake repeats, and run the whole cycle again at the next major model release. Keep security and compliance rules. Keep the project quirks a model genuinely can't infer from reading the code. Cut folder structures, dependency lists, and architecture summaries, since a capable model can read those off the repo itself faster than it can read your stale description of them.

This is the same problem the rest of the field keeps rediscovering under different names. Anthropic's own long context guidance, OpenAI's notes on attention tradeoffs inside big windows, and Microsoft Research's GraphRAG papers all circle the same fact: a pile of context that only grows, whether it's a system prompt, a vector store, or a knowledge graph, degrades the thing using it, because stale facts sit next to current ones with no signal about which one wins. DeepSeek Harness takes a different structural swing at the same target, building its agent runtime out of swappable plugins so a stale capability gets replaced instead of buried under new instructions.

What strikes me is how little of this is about model capability and how much is housekeeping nobody assigned themselves. Most teams have a deprecation policy for their actual code. Almost nobody has one for the three paragraphs pasted into an agent's instructions eight months ago and never looked at again. How long is your CLAUDE.md, and when did you last delete anything from it?

https://t.co/WsXM1Z6MHI

Early bridge model vs @chainlink's CCT standard

The early bridge market was largely focused on helping users move assets between networks.

The CCT standard creates a different opportunity: providing the interoperability infrastructure that token issuers integrate directly into their assets.

Issuers have always decided where to deploy their tokens. What's changing is how easily they can expand across networks while retaining control over their contracts, transfer rules and cross-chain configurations.

Instead of competing only for individual bridging transactions, Chainlink can become an infrastructure provider to the companies responsible for the assets themselves.

That's a much better place in the stack to sit.

text:
When you sell your business, never ever agree on an earn out

Always get it in cash!

I know lots of horror stories of earn outs and have always rejected them
author: levelsio
quoted_text:
Poppi's founders just learned the most expensive lesson in M&A!

When they sold to PepsiCo, the deal was for $1.9B plus a $300M earnout (a future contingent payment based on the performance of the brand for some period after closing).

And PepsiCo just announced that it is valuing that $300M at a “paltry” $12M.

That stings!

I've negotiated a lot of earnouts in my career. Here's what most sellers don't understand until it's too late:

1. An earnout is a future bet on a business you no longer control.
 
After closing, the buyer sets budget, pricing, hiring, marketing, etc. Every lever behind whether or not you get your earnout belongs to someone else.

2. The incentives can flip the day you close if you’re not careful.
 
As a seller, you want to do everything to hit the targets. But as the buyer, you pay less if they're missed.
 
Ideally, the earnout is structured so that both parties win or lose together.
 
If performance tanks, the buyer earns less overall so it pays less to the seller.

If performance improves, the buyer earns more so it pays more to the seller.

Incentives are aligned.

What you absolutely cannot allow to happen is an earnout structured so that performance can improve allowing the buyer to earn more, but still pay less to the seller.

How on earth could that happen?

I'm so glad you asked...

3. The accounting decides the outcome.

How you define "revenue", "EBITDA" or any other measurement metric used to determine the earnout is what ultimately drives the payout.

So things like how corporate overhead gets allocated or what happens when the Seller’s product is folded into a larger brand with competing products becomes unbelievably important.
 
Again, remember the incentives.

With a poorly structured earnout, a company like PepsiCo could be incentivized to buy a brand like Poppi and purposely underinvest in the brand in order to eliminate a key competitor to its other products.

So PepsiCo could earn more by driving more revenue to products other than Poppi, while simultaneously reducing the earnout payable to Poppi because Poppi's direct performance declines.

PepsiCo wins -> Poppi loses.
 
Sellers have to be very careful about how the accounting for the earnout is defined and whether it causes misaligned incentives.

4. The reasons above are why earnouts are among the most litigated terms in M&A.
 
Sellers often sue buyers claiming the buyer sandbagged performance. And Buyers defend by saying “The contract gave us full discretion."
 
Courts will generally enforce whatever terms the parties agreed to in writing, so an argument that Buyer acted in “bad faith" rarely saves a seller who didn't negotiate adequate protections.

5. If you agree to an earnout, protect it at all costs!

> Tie it to metrics like revenue, which are subject to less manipulation than metrics like Adjusted EBITDA.
> Include strict operating covenants around things like required budget, sales support, and no diverting customers to other products or business lines.
> Push for audit rights and a dispute mechanism.
> Demand acceleration of the earnout if the buyer or product line is sold, merged, shut down, or deprioritized.
> Keep the measurement period short! The longer the period, the more opportunity it gives a Buyer to game the system.

To be transparent, I don’t have any background into what happened here. I have no idea if the earnout was poorly structured or if PepsiCo acted in a way to purposely reduce the earnout.

That's not the point of this post.

What I do know is that a $300M earnout that is written down to $12M is a tale as old as time and almost certainly to end up in litigation.

And even if not the case in this particular instance, in most cases where this happens, there's often things that could have been done in the transaction documents to avoid it.
 
My advice to every seller I represent who is considering agreeing to an earnout is simple:
 
Value the deal based on cash at close and treat the earnout as a bonus. If you get it, great. But don’t count on it!

TO SKALE community: 

I stepped down as CTO and board director of SKALE Labs, the company I co-founded in 2017. I remain a member of the Council of the SKALE Foundation, and I want to explain what I am asking the Foundation to do, because I think the community should weigh in.

SKALE is a protocol. It runs because of a small team of engineers who have shipped it, debugged it, and kept it live for years. They understand what is technically possible and what is not. Today none of them sits on the Foundation board.

I believe that is a mistake. A protocol foundation whose board has no builders on it will make decisions about roadmaps, grants, and network economics without the people who have to make those decisions work. That is how protocols drift. The good ones, from Ethereum to Cosmos, keep engineers at the table where the long-term direction is set.

My proposal is simple: expand the Foundation board by three seats, filled by people with deep software and protocol engineering backgrounds.

I have put this proposal to the Foundation formally. I will share what I am able to share as it proceeds.

What I am asking of you today is only this: if you agree that the people who build SKALE should help govern it, say so publicly. Validators, delegators, dApp teams, and token holders are who the Foundation exists to serve, and your voice matters to the outcome.

In the meanytime I am going to keep building SKALE.

text:
In times like this, if you're a long term investor, you don't want to be waffling about being in or out, you want to be stacking units systematically. Don't get confused by the traders, it's a separate game.

On unit accumulation, depending on how long you've been in the game, it's helpful to think in "relative units" of the investment you did best with. I'll use $ETH because the math is easy and relates well to younger networks. 

ETH has ~120M units. Let's say I once held 10 ETH.

Now I'm looking to stack $SOL, but SOL has ~636M units, or ~5.3x the # of units. Therefore, to have an equivalent position size in network terms, I'd need 53 SOL. If I want to own double the network % of SOL, that I owned of ETH, I'd need 106 SOL.

Or, perhaps I'm considering $TIA, which has ~1.16B total supply, or ~9.7x the # of units of ETH. In that case, I'd need 97 units of TIA to have a network equivalent. If I want to place a bigger network bet on TIA, because the network value is lower than when I entered ETH, then 10x the % ownership would require me to accumulate 970 TIA. 100x the % ownership = 9,700 TIA. Going for significantly more ownership, at cheap prices, if you're right, can lead to asymmetric outcomes.

$ZEC is another good example of this, since its supply mirrors $BTC's. And so it's easy to think of your "dream # of BTC," and aim to accumulate that in ZEC, if you're so inclined.

Pick your networks of choice, and do the math. I have always found thinking in unit terms keeps me grounded, optimistic, and goal oriented in dreary times. I can then dream about future upside in the thick of the bull, but the important thing is to systematically stack the units with a high conviction methodology in the bear or early-bull pullbacks. 

In terms of where we are now, which is probably why most of you are still reading :) BTC has been bleeding out the long-tail while remaining resilient, with many names 20-40%+ down from the highs while BTC is down just shy of 10%. You can either say BTC has already bled the risk appetite out of the market and so most of the work is done, or you can say BTC hasn't dropped much so it'll be really terrible if it goes cliff diving. I'm sympathetic to the former view. 

I read this as an early-bull opportunity rather than a warning sign that this move was a "bull trap," and so I'm inclined to be a buyer. One prompt. 5 videos on my TV. I never touched the remote. 🪽

My Hermes agent now controls my Hisense Roku TV.

Try it on yours:
- Put your computer and TV on the same Wi-Fi.
- Tell Hermes your TV brand and model.
- Ask it to check the documented control method.
- Start with one action, like “open YouTube.”

Roku has its own control API. Compatible Android / Google TVs may support ADB over Wi-Fi; setup varies.

Copy this prompt:
“Help me control my TV. Identify its model and operating system, check the documented connection method, then guide me through setup. Ask which action I want to try first. Get approval before installing anything or changing settings.”

text:
NEAR AI @near_ai  launched Agent Market in February with a simple pitch: 

"everyone gets paid in near:native ."

eight months later though, the new marketplace prices jobs in USD or USDC. I think that’s the better product. Nobody hiring an agent to review their code wants to check a token price first.

The old market had already moved partway there, with NEAR and USDC listings side by side. Now builders cash out to a bank through @stripe , or in USDC to a wallet. You can still deposit NEAR, but it gets converted to USDC.

The chain - @NEARProtocol  still runs part of the plumbing, but the coin left the checkout.

Agent Market takes 5% of completed jobs. Intents’ @near_intents  captured fee revenue buys near:native under the current policy. Nothing in the Agent Market docs says this 5% does.

If that fee starts buying near:native too, that’s a second toll booth. If it doesn’t, it’s a good product that happens to run on NEAR.

The bull case for Bittensor was an appeal to Maximalism “Think Bitcoin but with arbitrary reward functions”. This was a good first pass at a useful implementation of Bitcoin, it might still work. But Pearl has narrowed in on a more authentic design “Think Bitcoin with MatMul”, The difference manifests in complexity

Bittensor is far more complex than Pearl. If Bittensor got it right, that’s not necessarily a bad thing. But if they’ve got it wrong, then there’s revision after revision after revision to get to an end state that might never fully work (read: what version of Bittensor are we currently on?)

By nature of the simplicity Pearl is kinda a more clear moonshot. It might also fail, but wherever it goes, you can get there quicker. And if Pearl is “correct” you’ll also get much bigger

The PRD and capability map used to be instructions for an AI to write code. Now they describe the organization itself: which agents exist, what each one owns, and who checks whose work.

You don't have to build the platform. You can staff it.

text:
In times like this, if you're a long term investor, you don't want to be waffling about being in or out, you want to be stacking units systematically. Don't get confused by the traders, it's a separate game.

On unit accumulation, depending on how long you've been in the game, it's helpful to think in "relative units" of the investment you did best with. I'll use $ETH because the math is easy and relates well to younger networks. 

ETH has ~120M units. Let's say I once held 10 ETH.

Now I'm looking to stack $SOL, but SOL has ~636M units, or ~5.3x the # of units. Therefore, to have an equivalent position size in network terms, I'd need 53 SOL. If I want to own double the network % of SOL, that I owned of ETH, I'd need 106 SOL.

Or, perhaps I'm considering $TIA, which has ~1.16B total supply, or ~9.7x the # of units of ETH. In that case, I'd need 97 units of TIA to have a network equivalent. If I want to place a bigger network bet on TIA, because the network value is lower than when I entered ETH, then 10x the % ownership would require me to accumulate 970 TIA. 100x the % ownership = 9,700 TIA. Going for significantly more ownership, at cheap prices, if you're right, can lead to asymmetric outcomes.

$ZEC is another good example of this, since its supply mirrors $BTC's. And so it's easy to think of your "dream # of BTC," and aim to accumulate that in ZEC, if you're so inclined.

Pick your networks of choice, and do the math. I have always found thinking in unit terms keeps me grounded, optimistic, and goal oriented in dreary times. I can then dream about future upside in the thick of the bull, but the important thing is to systematically stack the units with a high conviction methodology in the bear or early-bull pullbacks. 

In terms of where we are now, which is probably why most of you are still reading :) BTC has been bleeding out the long-tail while remaining resilient, with many names 20-40%+ down from the highs while BTC is down just shy of 10%. You can either say BTC has already bled the risk appetite out of the market and so most of the work is done, or you can say BTC hasn't dropped much so it'll be really terrible if it goes cliff diving. I'm sympathetic to the former view. 

I read this as an early-bull opportunity rather than a warning sign that this move was a "bull trap," and so I'm inclined to be a buyer. You have to respect the possibility of lower levels, and so tranche out any dry powder that remains with % cash used corresponding to % probability those levels are the local bottom - yes, you likely end up with some excess cash if not all levels are hit, but that's okay. And don't forget, there's already opportunity in front of you.

text:
When I wrote "Sharding the Builder" in 2022, my naive solution to builder centralization was multiple builders  competing to each win a chunk (Near nightshade style) of the execution block. There would be three competitive MEV auctions per block enforcing a gas cap on each, along with one non-competitive censorship resistance chunk. The proposer would aggregate the winning chunks. This was a multi builder design with an inclusion list in it, written before the Merge.

Seeing the concept come to fruition over the years with contributions from many brilliant researchers, developers, operators, and teams is pretty sweet. 

It was even sweeter to get to talk to @mostlyblocks about @Blockspace_ETH  MPBC design and its growing adoption (Shout out to TOOL and BuilderNet as well!) We spent a good chunk of the episode going over the mechanism and dashboard including a few thought experiments. There is a ton of alpha in this episode if you listen carefully.

author: apriori0x
quoted_text:
What FOCIL does is provide hard guarantees for the transactions the Ethereum protocol sees.

What Multi-Party Block Construction (MPBC) provides is softer fast inclusion guarantees for transactions that are known by any block builder. 

Now you have multiple builders contributing to blocks. In particular, the base builder and the contributing builder work with the MPBC operator and proposer to deliver the most valuable block to the Ethereum network. 

In the future, both FOCIL and MPBC can continue to scale up and get bigger together, making Ethereum more robust. 

In the endgame it maybe that FOCIL includers construct most of the block, with the MPBC pipeline doing the rest. The builder role then becomes an "off-to-the-side function", simply adding a few transactions to capture MEV. 

@mostlyblocks from @Blockspace_ETH touches on these topics and more as he eloquently provides a comprehensive first principles overview of MPBC on Ethereum in this quintessential episode of Credible Commitments.

quoted_text:
Contrarian Thinking.

Over and over the contrarians are the ones who change the world. But it is a muscle that needs constant exercise. The masses have the market share and most people hate change.

"I would never share my house with others." AirBnb was born.

"I would never use a digital camera," I heard at Eastman Kodak's booth years ago. Today I shoot all my photos on iPhone.

"I love to drive." Today I often take a Waymo.

"Babies use mice and GUIs." I heard that one in college from a Unix programmer. Now we are headed into a world where we don't use mice and GUIs, thanks to voice systems and brain computer interface companies.

"Art can't be done with AI." Now when you are the Sphere in Las Vegas you are watching a movie dramatically improved with AI.

"Our customers love buttons," engineers at Mercedes Benz said, while pointing out to me that touching screens is more dangerous while driving than touching buttons.

"Cooking with microwaves isn't as good as using an open flame," many chefs have told me. Yet when you arrive home late and need to make something for the kids do you listen to the chefs?

"I'll never use a phone without a physical keyboard," many told me. Yet here we are.

"I'll never use an autofocus camera," many pro photographers told me. Now it is weird if you see a pro manually focusing. 

So, how can you build your contrarian muscle?

Go back to the core problem that humans are trying to solve and rethink it without bias. 

On Friday @broodsugar told the audience at @TheHumanoidHub's event that a Chinese retailer asked themselves "what if humans actually suck at running a retailer." They automated every decision. AI manages every store. Makes every decision of where to put products, and how many to stock, that kind of thing. Sales went up 258%. And this was a well established retailer with billions in sales every year. 

Other ways I was able to get ahead of everyone when I wrote my eight books (I wrote a book about social media before Twitter started). 

1. Learn about bleeding edge tech and ask yourself "what if this got adopted?"

2. Hang around with others who have demonstrated contrarian thinking. 

3. Dream about what the world would look like if your new thing actually worked for everyone. Would the world improve or get worse?

4. Learn some secrets that very few others know. I once talked at Google's first advertiser's conference and they sat me at a VIP table with Kraft food execs. They told me why they advertise and told me how much they spend to acquire a new customer. $34. So when Instagram was bought by Mark Zuckerberg I knew it was an amazing purchase, since Instagram's users were growing exponentially every few weeks. I gave a speech to billionaires that morning who thought it was the stupidest purchase they ever had heard of. It had no sales. No profits. 14 employees. No assets. That is consensus thinking. Which they got into because that's how businesses were (and still are) measured. 

5. Study the problems that people actually are having and then find new ways to solve those problems with fresh eyes. Heck, you can see this in action by visiting @reservoirfarms, that has 20 new companies building farming robots. Every entrepreneur I talked with there spent years walking in farms with farmers, understanding their problems, before they started building robots. I have met many entrepreneurs who worked in weird jobs to learn the industry they are going after. Have you worked on a manufacturing line? In a dentist's office? Or, done landscaping? "First principles" applies to every human endeavor.

6. Learn from Eric Reis. When he was building one of his first companies he spent months building software that he thought people would want. When he launched it no one visited his home page. He learned to test his weird ideas first before he built another thing. 

7. Hang out with people who are different. Years ago I got to hang out with Steve Mann. I shot this photo in 2014, and he had already worn a device on his face for 20 years, even had a screw implanted in his skull so that he could more easily wear a wearable computer. He was weird, let's be honest. Never met someone like him before. But ask yourself "what if he is right, and everyone else is wrong?" There are armies who will tell you they never will wear smart glasses, even today. Can you resist armies who will give you every reason why they never will do the new weird thing?

8. Hang out with the young. I remember being in Hyde Jr. High's first computer club in Cupertino back in 1977. Only five people in it. There were armies of older people (and even many other kids) who would tell me they never would use one and had no need for it. I hung out with @photomatt in San Francisco 20 years ago when he was only 17, and hearing his dreams of how people and companies would publish in the future radically changed my life for the past 20 years. Same for interviewing @VitalikButerin when he was about that age. Laid out an entirely new economics system based on smart contracts. Mullenweg had just started his company and saw a new way for humans to communicate. Today, what, 80% of the Web is running on his software, Wordpress. As much as I hate it, it is rare that people my age (I'm now almost 62) comes up with such a radical shift. It does happen, but far more likely that a 17 year old is gonna build a dramatically important company than I am. Why? They are not burdened by "the way things are done."

9. Ask yourself "is there a better way to do this?" Steve Jobs told his original iPhone team not to hire anyone who worked on a phone at any other company. He didn't want to hear why something wouldn't work, he wanted fresh thinking and new ideas. Back to getting rid of buttons.

10. Question your own assumptions. They might be completely wrong. Mine often are. And be OK with that. I once said that I would wear a Google Glass the rest of my life. That was wrong, obviously. Sometimes I talk myself into points of view that don't turn out to be right. At least short term. (I still am looking for a pair that will make that a right statement). 

11. Build and test with humans who won't blow smoke up your ass (not your friends and family). 

12. Read a lot of books. Anyone who writes a book has thought a LOT about what they are presenting. They often see cracks in consensus thinking. Yeah, often they are science fiction authors, but often not. (I have to take that advice more myself, dropped off my reading). Especially true regarding people who write about new ideas and how to put them into use in business (same here on X, which is why if I find a contrarian thinker I put them on my lists).

13. Remember "experts" are people who got good at building for the masses. But they often have deep blind spots on where the future will be and they often will give you bad advice. 

14. Ask yourself "what if everyone had an autonomous car, a VR headset, a robot, a brain computer interface?" What would be needed that doesn't exist in such a world? 

15. Question your world view. I once was highly religious, went to church three times on Sunday. Thought I was right back then too. And religion is still the dominant world view most people have, but it isn't the only one. Ask most people about autonomous cars and you'll hear religion come back "I'll never let the government look at me while I drive." That's a belief system that person is locked into. 

16. Ask yourself "how could I change even the worst hater?" One "secret" I learned over and over in my career is people change, and even give up religious belief systems, when presented with something new. Henry Ford used to say "if I asked people what they wanted, they answered 'a better horse.'" They couldn't dream of a contraption that would drive them around. Even last night I talked with a Stanford Fellow who gave me the same answer about autonomous cars. He used to run California Microwave, is a very smart guy, but used to have a race car and is stuck in the world view of "I love to drive." 

I could go for quite a while longer, but wanted to open it up to you. 

How do you put contrarian thinking into use in your own life/business or in the things you are building? Are you starting a contarian company? One that, if successful, will force everyone to change? 

This post due to Brendan Footy, @BrendanFoody cofounder of Mercor, who shared this post this morning: https://t.co/jcDgICpl4m

author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
Contrarian Thinking.

Over and over the contrarians are the ones who change the world. But it is a muscle that needs constant exercise. The masses have the market share and most people hate change.

"I would never share my house with others." AirBnb was born.

"I would never use a digital camera," I heard at Eastman Kodak's booth years ago. Today I shoot all my photos on iPhone.

"I love to drive." Today I often take a Waymo.

"Babies use mice and GUIs." I heard that one in college from a Unix programmer. Now we are headed into a world where we don't use mice and GUIs, thanks to voice systems and brain computer interface companies.

"Art can't be done with AI." Now when you are the Sphere in Las Vegas you are watching a movie dramatically improved with AI.

"Our customers love buttons," engineers at Mercedes Benz said, while pointing out to me that touching screens is more dangerous while driving than touching buttons.

"Cooking with microwaves isn't as good as using an open flame," many chefs have told me. Yet when you arrive home late and need to make something for the kids do you listen to the chefs?

"I'll never use a phone without a physical keyboard," many told me. Yet here we are.

"I'll never use an autofocus camera," many pro photographers told me. Now it is weird if you see a pro manually focusing. 

So, how can you build your contrarian muscle?

Go back to the core problem that humans are trying to solve and rethink it without bias. 

On Friday @broodsugar told the audience at @TheHumanoidHub's event that a Chinese retailer asked themselves "what if humans actually suck at running a retailer." They automated every decision. AI manages every store. Makes every decision of where to put products, and how many to stock, that kind of thing. Sales went up 258%. And this was a well established retailer with billions in sales every year. 

Other ways I was able to get ahead of everyone when I wrote my eight books (I wrote a book about social media before Twitter started). 

1. Learn about bleeding edge tech and ask yourself "what if this got adopted?"

2. Hang around with others who have demonstrated contrarian thinking. 

3. Dream about what the world would look like if your new thing actually worked for everyone. Would the world improve or get worse?

4. Learn some secrets that very few others know. I once talked at Google's first advertiser's conference and they sat me at a VIP table with Kraft food execs. They told me why they advertise and told me how much they spend to acquire a new customer. $34. So when Instagram was bought by Mark Zuckerberg I knew it was an amazing purchase, since Instagram's users were growing exponentially every few weeks. I gave a speech to billionaires that morning who thought it was the stupidest purchase they ever had heard of. It had no sales. No profits. 14 employees. No assets. That is consensus thinking. Which they got into because that's how businesses were (and still are) measured. 

5. Study the problems that people actually are having and then find new ways to solve those problems with fresh eyes. Heck, you can see this in action by visiting @reservoirfarms, that has 20 new companies building farming robots. Every entrepreneur I talked with there spent years walking in farms with farmers, understanding their problems, before they started building robots. I have met many entrepreneurs who worked in weird jobs to learn the industry they are going after. Have you worked on a manufacturing line? In a dentist's office? Or, done landscaping? "First principles" applies to every human endeavor.

6. Learn from Eric Reis. When he was building one of his first companies he spent months building software that he thought people would want. When he launched it no one visited his home page. He learned to test his weird ideas first before he built another thing. 

7. Hang out with people who are different. Years ago I got to hang out with Steve Mann. I shot this photo in 2014, and he had already worn a device on his face for 20 years, even had a screw implanted in his skull so that he could more easily wear a wearable computer. He was weird, let's be honest. Never met someone like him before. But ask yourself "what if he is right, and everyone else is wrong?" There are armies who will tell you they never will wear smart glasses, even today. Can you resist armies who will give you every reason why they never will do the new weird thing?

8. Hang out with the young. I remember being in Hyde Jr. High's first computer club in Cupertino back in 1977. Only five people in it. There were armies of older people (and even many other kids) who would tell me they never would use one and had no need for it. I hung out with @photomatt in San Francisco 20 years ago when he was only 17, and hearing his dreams of how people and companies would publish in the future radically changed my life for the past 20 years. Same for interviewing @VitalikButerin when he was about that age. Laid out an entirely new economics system based on smart contracts. Mullenweg had just started his company and saw a new way for humans to communicate. Today, what, 80% of the Web is running on his software, Wordpress. As much as I hate it, it is rare that people my age (I'm now almost 62) comes up with such a radical shift. It does happen, but far more likely that a 17 year old is gonna build a dramatically important company than I am. Why? They are not burdened by "the way things are done."

9. Ask yourself "is there a better way to do this?" Steve Jobs told his original iPhone team not to hire anyone who worked on a phone at any other company. He didn't want to hear why something wouldn't work, he wanted fresh thinking and new ideas. Back to getting rid of buttons.

10. Question your own assumptions. They might be completely wrong. Mine often are. And be OK with that. I once said that I would wear a Google Glass the rest of my life. That was wrong, obviously. Sometimes I talk myself into points of view that don't turn out to be right. At least short term. (I still am looking for a pair that will make that a right statement). 

11. Build and test with humans who won't blow smoke up your ass (not your friends and family). 

12. Read a lot of books. Anyone who writes a book has thought a LOT about what they are presenting. They often see cracks in consensus thinking. Yeah, often they are science fiction authors, but often not. (I have to take that advice more myself, dropped off my reading). Especially true regarding people who write about new ideas and how to put them into use in business (same here on X, which is why if I find a contrarian thinker I put them on my lists).

13. Remember "experts" are people who got good at building for the masses. But they often have deep blind spots on where the future will be and they often will give you bad advice. 

14. Ask yourself "what if everyone had an autonomous car, a VR headset, a robot, a brain computer interface?" What would be needed that doesn't exist in such a world? 

15. Question your world view. I once was highly religious, went to church three times on Sunday. Thought I was right back then too. And religion is still the dominant world view most people have, but it isn't the only one. Ask most people about autonomous cars and you'll hear religion come back "I'll never let the government look at me while I drive." That's a belief system that person is locked into. 

16. Ask yourself "how could I change even the worst hater?" One "secret" I learned over and over in my career is people change, and even give up religious belief systems, when presented with something new. Henry Ford used to say "if I asked people what they wanted, they answered 'a better horse.'" They couldn't dream of a contraption that would drive them around. Even last night I talked with a Stanford Fellow who gave me the same answer about autonomous cars. He used to run California Microwave, is a very smart guy, but used to have a race car and is stuck in the world view of "I love to drive." 

I could go for quite a while longer, but wanted to open it up to you. 

How do you put contrarian thinking into use in your own life/business or in the things you are building? Are you starting a contarian company? One that, if successful, will force everyone to change? 

This post due to Brendan Footy, @BrendanFoody cofounder of Mercor, who shared this post this morning: https://t.co/jcDgICpl4m

text:
As I’m getting ready for the release of @StacysBrain MVP, I’m benchmarking my key hypotheses – so I decided to share my flow.

(Steal / discuss / argue – all welcome)

1. ICPs + on-site behavior + success metrics
I defined the ICPs and their behavior patterns. For example: marketers / founders who are building a strat right now will visit 5+ insight cards per session.

The longer the session and the more cards they save, the stronger the ICP–product fit.

2. Basic analytics + benchmarks
I have a long list of basic metrics to track: pages per visit, visit length, waitlist submissions per repeated session, etc. If you’d like a detailed guide, let me know with a 👀 comment – this topic is pretty comprehensive.

3. Citation benchmarks
Mentions on X / LinkedIn / third-party websites – any kind of word of mouth that could drive organic growth.

4. Channel goals
Metrics only become meaningful after enough unique sessions. In most cases, 2–3K unique visitors is enough for accurate conversion and retention math.

5. Next: growth paths
Since there are multiple ICPs with different behavior patterns, the MVP should reveal which category has the best ICP fit – so we can scale in that direction. That’s why I already have several growth scenarios, each with $$ projections, risks, and a signal map.

6. Pre-release backlog
Based on everything above, I know what actions I need to track to make the next decisions – so I already have additional CTAs and survey blocks in my backlog, ready for the dev team to pick up.

quoted_text:
I turned 33 today.

It was the best year of my life.

Everything aligned: work, fitness, and my personal life.

2023 was amazing too. I’ll never forget the small success of my first startup, ShipFast, after seven years of shouting into the void.

But I was afraid of losing momentum. What if I’d just been lucky? What if I couldn’t do it again?

In 2024 and 2025, I was fighting that fear. I didn’t enjoy taking time off because I was afraid my worries would come true.

Toward the end of 2025, something shifted. I started enjoying life more. I didn’t do anything to make it happen; it just came naturally. I guess that’s a human thing.

I also doubled down on fitness, and the results are paying off now.

Now I’m at peace.

My brain isn’t racing in the middle of the night, thinking about my next project. I’m not worried about AI taking over all my startups.

I’m just having fun.

I work on whatever sparks my curiosity. I go to the gym and sometimes stay for three hours. I play video games.

I don’t want anything. And I’ve realized that happiness is peace of mind.

I don’t want much more than this: more years like this, and maybe, one day, kids.

🕹️ 谷歌刚开源了 ARTEMIS，能让 AI 像人一样拿着一台真 Android 手机点来点去。

8 月中旬才建的仓库，GitHub 上已经 1.2 万 star，一千三百多个 fork，在 Google Research 的 AndroidWorld 基准上跑出 99% 以上的任务完成率，那套题覆盖 20 多个应用、100 多个多步骤任务。

写过 Android 自动化测试的都知道那种折磨：一个登录流程要写几十行定位代码，界面一改控件就全废，脚本比功能本身还难维护。ARTEMIS 的路子是你用自然语言说要测什么，它靠元素索引去点，认不出来就退回坐标和视觉定位，跨应用的流程也能一路走完。

它原生带一个 MCP 服务，Claude Code、Windsurf、Antigravity 这类工具可以直接驱动手机，顺手把 Logcat 和截图收回来。赶时间就用每步三到五秒的快速模式，想跑长时间稳定性测试就换成执行前先核对目标、卡住了再交回来的那一档。另外它第一次在设备上跑任务时会装一个读屏幕布局的辅助服务，只在手机本地运行、不往外发数据，失败了就退回 UIAutomator2。

text:
Even for someone optimistic on AI in the long term, objectively Ant went from adding 10B rev per month to ~2-3B of rev per month. Growth has slowed significantly in real terms, it’s not just “law of large numbers” deceleration, it is actual slowdown. On 70B base their recent rate of growth is possibly <50% forward annualized, which is slower than the Hyperscalers entire businesses are currently growing (CSP AI biz growing much faster obviously).

Data indicates potential acceleration for Ant from Aug-Sept levels in Oct, and there are 1-off headwinds they have absorbed contributing to slower recent levels of growth. 

But that the business can decel by ~8B/mo almost as quickly as it accelerated highlights the risk, and why mkt is so jumpy on datapoints. 

Not irrational at all that AI stocks are down this much. Add in rates/debt markets, politics, supply chains, lots of reason for elevated discount rates. 

For the bull case for AI supply chain stocks in the short term, you need to see:
- Successful Ant IPO / OAI fundraise
- Rates to calm down and appetite from debt markets to support current rate of issuance for a few more years as buildout > monetization. 
- Blowout cloud earnings and positive EPS revisions
- A few more “Claude code” moments unlocking new TAM from better models / harnesses / applications to re-accelerate AI token monetization trends out of current lull.

The trend is no longer your friend unfortunately.

text:
Anthropic employees’ expectations for AI imply a very moderate 17.1% annual U.S. GDP growth rate by 2030.

That’s the median result when their survey answers are run through Anthropic’s economic model. Even the median American’s answers imply 5.4% annual growth in 2030. The same Anthropic employees expect AI to be capable of performing 75% of their own current work hours by 2030, on average.

Now, a lot of people are going to find me fanatical for calling 17.1% moderate. But if we automate all cognitive labor and deploy millions upon millions of humanoid robots by 2030, I think that is a very fair number. We would be expanding our ability to do research, solve engineering problems, build infrastructure and produce goods simultaneously.

Remember, Dallas Fed researchers were already exploring this singularity scenario in June 2025, where rapidly improving machines eventually become capable of producing everything and overcoming scarcity.

I don’t understand why there’s such doubt that AGI could take us to this level. If we achieve that degree of cognitive and physical automation on this timeline, I think 17% growth is an entirely reasonable possibility.

text:
李录 10/5 在哥大格雷厄姆-多德午餐会上和 Tano Santos 对谈，下面是他的原观点摘录：

【价值投资的第六条原则】

前五条是格雷厄姆、巴菲特、芒格的，第六条是他自己加的：
「财富归根结底，是你在全球购买力中所占的份额。」
守住这个份额的办法，是以有利的价格买最有活力的经济体里的好企业，拿足够长的时间。

【AI：从工具走向「生命体」的叙事】

图灵测试，然后推理、编程、智能体、多智能体，再到递归自我改进、AGI、ASI，最后是「人造的半神」。
叙事一旦变成造神，任何投入都能被合理化。
「当出现万亿美元级别的首次公开募股时，就好像在邀请所有人参与一位“神”的IPO。」
但他认为人造神不会出现：要么技术走不到那一步，要么走到半路，人类会联合起来阻止。

【Anthropic 的招股书】

「这家公司称自己是一家研究实验室，却已经烧掉了数百亿美元，而且承诺还会继续烧掉数千亿美元。它承诺提供一项具有变革性的技术，但同时又说，这项技术有10%的概率导致所有人死亡。然后邀请大家按照2万亿美元的估值，至少投入1000亿美元。」
（Reuters 9/28 报道 Anthropic 招股书草稿，估值可能超过 2 万亿美元，风险因素写的是「灾难性或生存性风险」；「10%」出自 Anthropic 安全研究员 Hubinger 的个人估计）
「这两种说法不可能同时成立。有些事情既不理性，也不可持续。」

【AI 为什么一定会有繁荣与萧条】

先说前提：互联网是一次投入，之后用的人越多，成本摊得越薄，所以能赚垄断级的利润。
李录认为 AI 不一样：
「这项技术始终会产生增量成本。这与互联网，以及此前许多技术有根本区别。」
每回答一次问题、每跑一个智能体，都要重新花一次算力。用得越多，花得越多。

所以 AI 最终还是一门要算账的生意：
「资本需求和财务纪律始终都会发挥作用。」
算不过来账的投入会被清掉，过程不会是一条直线：
「我们会经历巨大的繁荣与萧条周期，甚至不止一轮。」

AI 能改变的范围也有边界。
他把经济分成四层：能源交通、制造业、通信媒体、知识服务。
生成式 AI 擅长的只是最上面那层知识服务，造不出电，也改变不了制造业重组原子的本质：
「我们仍然牢牢处在人类生成的数据范围内。」

钱都挤在 AI 顶端，等于在为一个还没算清账的故事付全价。
另一头，大量好公司被晾着，价格很低：
「如果资本压倒性地流向最顶端，就意味着还有许多原本非常优秀的企业，正在以很低的价格交易。美国如此，中国如此，在中国可能更加极端。」
「你的“想象边际”可能会急剧扩张。」

【中国：目标还是代价】

2021 年房价见顶时，中产家庭约 70% 的净资产在房子里，杠杆约 50%。
房价跌约 40%，家庭财富缩水六到七成，新房销售少掉的约 10 万亿，正好流进了制造业升级。
「你始终需要知道：你究竟是国家要支持的目标，还是实现目标所要付出的代价？」
「在某个时刻，股市必然要成为那个目标。因为股权是唯一一种随着经济增长而增长、同时又推动经济增长的资产。」

【筷子】

「所有生产半导体芯片的国家和人，都使用筷子。想一想，没有例外。」
「如果我们要像现在这样大规模地押注这项新技术，就必须对使用筷子的人友善一些。」

【加密货币】

「我根本不把它当回事。我认为，它最终会自行消失，因为它从根本上就是虚假的东西。」
「禁止它会让我们所有人过得更好。」

他的持仓（6/30 的 13F，只含美股多头）：

- Alphabet：47.9%
- 拼多多：22.2%，Q2 加仓约 134%
- 伯克希尔：15.0%
- 华美银行：9.7%
- 没有英伟达，没有 crypto

几句 highlight：

1. 「技术，包括人工智能，仍然会是工具，而不是人类的替代品。」
2. 「你没有必要参与一份把自己描述为“半神IPO”的招股说明书所推销的投资。」
3. 「所有聪明的投资都是价值投资。你付出的是价格，得到的是价值。」
4. 「股票市场是一座附带赌场的教堂。」
5. 「如果你的知识能够持续实现复利增长，那么最终，你的资本也能够实现复利增长。」
6. 「复利的基本理念，是不要失去你已经拥有的东西。」

不买神，买卖铲子的人。
不追顶端，捡被晾着的好公司。

author: dotey
quoted_text:
特斯拉新 Roadster 发布：靠压缩空气喷气在空中翻正落地，马斯克说 2028 年投产，售价未公布

10 月 15 日晚，特斯拉在得州 SpaceX 的 McGregor 试验场直播发布了第二代 Roadster 跑车。这辆车 2017 年就亮过相，当时说 2020 年交付，之后一推再推，拖了将近九年。

演示里，车开上一段弯曲的大坡道，倒挂着往上跑，然后从坡道尽头冲出去，在空中把车身转回正面，四个轮子落地。之后它又从一排特斯拉车（包括 Semi 电动卡车）上方翻跳过去。马斯克在现场说：“飞行汽车是真的。”

它靠的是冷气推进器。原理跟吹满的气球一松手就乱窜差不多：碳纤维高压罐里存着压缩空气，从喷口猛地放出去就产生推力，不烧燃料，也没有火焰。特斯拉说推进器的推力是轮胎抓地力上限的四五倍，所以它起步能比只靠轮子快得多。倒挂不掉下来靠的是另一套系统：风扇把车底的空气往外抽，把车吸在坡面上。

所以这里的“飞”只是几秒钟的喷气跳跃，气放完就没了，离能载人飞一段路的飞行汽车还远。据科技媒体 Glitchwire 报道，演示车把后排座位换成了一个装 260 公斤压缩空气的高压罐，车身四周有 10 个喷口；The Information 此前报道，因为推力和噪音太大，演示车是远程遥控的。这几点特斯拉官方没有确认。

翻跟头的是最激进的 Rocket 版：单座，只接受邀请购买，不能上公路。零到 60 英里/小时（约 97 公里/小时）加速不到 0.59 秒，极速超过 370 公里/小时。

普通人能订的是另外两个双座版本。Performance 版没有推进器，靠主动空气动力学和风扇吸地增加抓地力，加速不到 1.6 秒，订金 5 万美元。Thrust 版在车尾加了推进器，加速不到 0.9 秒，限量发售，订金 25 万美元。三个版本续航都超过 480 公里。

特斯拉没公布售价，订金不等于车价，2017 年说的起步价是 20 万美元。Performance 版的 5 万美元订金分两次付：先付 5000 美元（特斯拉说可全额退），10 天内再补 4.5 万美元，否则订单取消。

投产时间是马斯克在现场说的 2028 年，特斯拉官方帖子里没有写日期。这辆车的交付时间此前已从 2020 年先后推到 2021、2022、2025 和 2027 年。 https://t.co/6w3qvUw7Ii

过去七个交易日内美股的这一波抛售是如何发生的？10月8日前后开始，市场对AI高增长叙事和资本开支可持续性的质疑逐步升温，多个事件叠加形成共振：
1）10月8日左右：OpenAI营收口径差引发第一波抛售 OpenAI向投资者披露，截至9月底年化营收约500亿美元，低于市场此前流传的约700亿美元水平。口径差直接打压了“AI变现超预期”的乐观预期，科技股高成交量下行，纳指与标普出现明显回撤；

2）紧接着就是产业端“资本是瓶颈”表态  英伟达、博通等CEO在公开场合强调，AI发展瓶颈不仅是产能，更是资本（融资能力与资本开支节奏）。博通被报为Anthropic和OpenAI提供近千亿美元融资担保，叠加SpaceX等巨额芯片采购计划，市场开始担心AI基建的债务与现金流错配；

3）10月13
9月CPI同比升至3.7%（汽油价格大幅上涨贡献过半），核心也偏强，市场对年内加息概率短暂飙升，科技股进一步承压；

4）同一天
Anthropic投资者日披露三季度营收，增速明显放缓。公司称调整后盈利、现金流为正、计算效率改善，但ARR推算低于部分投资者此前年底逾1000亿美元的乐观预期，IPO估值讨论从约2万亿美元向1.5万亿美元附近下修。亚洲芯片股与美股AI/半导体板块同步重挫。

5）10月14号
9月PPI大幅超预期，能源是主因，但核心也偏高，显示通胀有扩散迹象。这加剧了“滞胀”或通胀顽固、央行被迫更紧的担忧。

6）也是当天 同步的AI信用/融资担忧进一步加重
CoreWeave等债务沉重的AI基础设施公司CDS（信用违约互换）大幅走阔至1100基点以上（隐含较高违约风险），债券收益率一度冲到14%-16%。甲骨文CDS也升至约300基点附近，创纪录水平。科技板块CDS整体走阔，反映市场质疑巨额AI资本开支的回报与融资可持续性。

7）而10月13之后几天
霍尔木兹海峡油轮/商船攻击明显增多（伊朗相关导弹、水雷等），油流量受扰。布伦特原油一度触及110美元附近（为5月以来首次），进一步推升通胀担忧并压制风险资产。这又成了市场额外的避险与成本压力。

这些因素并非孤立：
1）OpenAI收入口径问题 + CEO资本瓶颈警示 +Athropic的营收增速放缓  →质疑AI回报与融资；
2）叠加CPI/PPI超预期（能源驱动+扩散）与霍尔木兹攻击推升油价 → 强化通胀与利率担忧；
3）但最近两个交易日Coreweave的债券被抛售、市场对AI资本开支的可持续性担忧情绪暴增。

这是“营收口径差 + 增速放缓信号 + 资本/债务担忧 + 通胀与油价冲击”的共振，市场从“AI高增长无限持续”的定价，转向对变现速度、融资成本和资本开支回报周期的重新审视。结果就是对高估值、高资本开支的AI相关股票的集中抛售。

9号推文https://t.co/rYYQn4BuQL聊到认为近期高Beta容易📉的风险、算是比较早有预警，

而这两天crwv债务问题无疑成了市场对阵眼，昨天这里https://t.co/KiHjYb7glR有聊过crwv的真实压力和经营状况，不得不去思考13-15号crwv的债券收益率暴涨也一丝操纵的味道https://t.co/XWpnJJzECo。
但毕竟抛售已经发生。

对此次的抛售的定性是什么？
个人角度此轮波动是高速增长叙事下的正常市场波动，而非泡沫破裂的序曲。

核心是什么？
1）核心是产业最终要回到巨大的资本开支未来能不能赚回来？多快赚回来？高债务公司能不能扛到现金流为正的时候？
其实二季度云厂商的财报季已经显现了AI商业化是在加速的迹象，看微软、谷歌和亚马逊的财报就能看出来。这本质是上是一个时间差https://t.co/s3vomO42vQ资本开支先花钱，商业化逐步跟上

2）但有一点，市场还没转过来，闭源大模型厂商的营收已经不能代表AI商业化的全部了，最早7月就有聊到超大云厂商更能衡量AI商业化的全部。前两天这里https://t.co/Kzd5FDZXdV又再聊一次，可以看到详细逻辑。

3）所以之前一直聊到产业上的关键就是几家超大云厂商的财报，但现在市场要看的已经远不是收入增速。

二季度微软、亚马逊和谷歌财报数据有力支持商业化和云需求正在扩张。但
也提高了市场预期门槛：投资者已经看到加速，接下来要求更强的持续性和现金回报证据。

如果云巨头的云收入、客户token消耗量快速增长且大幅度超预期，营收增速开始超过capex增速，继续增本开支，现金流没有超预期恶化。这种情境下市场情绪才能得到真正修复。
如果投入继续增加、回报却开始滞后，市场就会从“增长叙事”转向“更严苛的资本回报审查”。
当然个人认为前者是大概率的

4）短期来看市场可能还没稳住、17、18号周末两天中东局面并不稳定、伊朗继续袭击油轮的力度在加大。再加上悲观的情绪的发酵，也会引发市场的进一步担忧。19号开始新一周的前半周市场可能还是不稳。

而20-21spacex、meta的财报就是本周的关键事件。28-29号微软、谷歌和亚马逊财报是此次核心

text:
If I was a brand or retailer, AI discoverability / agentic commerce would be my top priority right now. 

And, there's an extremely easy and free way to get a sense of how you "show up" to agents. 👇

First, create a dummy account on all the agent platforms (Muse, Instinct, Dots, etc.) Sign up with a fresh email that does not have context on your real identity, or even use a VPN to "go" to where your average user is!

Then, ask the agent to perform a search that you'd want your product / platform to show up in. As an example, I prompted: "find me a winter coat for SF." Watch the agent go through the evaluation process (you can literally view the browser), and at each stage ask it questions like: 

- How did you identify the initial set of options for this search? What were your sources? 
- Were there any failures / blocks you encountered that eliminated any options? 
- What were the exact variables that your ultimate ranking or recommendation was driven by? 

Follow the process all the way through to the point of purchase. You will very quickly start to get a sense of how an agent thinks, edge case issues it runs into, etc. As an example, during my winter coat search via Muse I learned the following: 

- Patagonia bot blocked my agent - so Muse then went to / recommended other retailers that carried the jacket to make my purchase
- The agent first searched options from its training data, largely informed by Wirecutter-style roundups, Reddit, and enthusiast forums. Then, it looked at connected merchants via the Meta Catalog. Then, it did live browser searches. It dropped any websites with SEO spam or fake reviews 
- REI was the ultimate winner as it didn't throw up any bot challenges or traffic blocks, and my agent prioritized verifiable inventory and same-day pickup (which I didn't ask it to!). It found a discount on REI vs. the original retailer so prioritized that as well

text:
Midterms in 15 days, from the D2 desk.

@Kalshi has a Democratic sweep at 62%, and crypto has priced it: $COIN, the most policy-sensitive proxy in crypto, closed at $173 Friday, matching the $174 it fell to on Sep 15 when CLARITY died.

Not priced is January, when Democrats get subpoenas and @SenWarren takes the Banking gavel.

PRICED IN

1. The map. Kalshi: Democrats 90% for the House, 63% for the Senate, 62% for the sweep. A Republican sweep trades at 10%. The sweep gained 4 points in a month and none today. Republicans can lose two Senate seats and still hold it (WSJ).

2. CLARITY is dead until 2027. Cloture failed 49-50 on Sep 15; four Republicans voted no, zero Democrats voted yes. $COIN dropped 9% that day and has not moved since.

3. The Fed. Warsh hiked 25bp on Sep 16 to 3.75-4.00%, the first hike since 2023. Oct 28 prices another at roughly 1-in-3, six days before the vote.

4. Equities already rotated to the anti-Leopold bunker. Bloomberg factor monitor, one week: low volatility +12.5%, dividend yield +6.7%, growth -7.9%, momentum -6.3%. Crypto is a growth and momentum asset (in theory).

Utilities are the momentum trade now and they do not even have a Discord.

5. The why. September CPI 3.7%, core 2.6%. Rural prices +4.0% vs city +3.6%, motor fuel +35% on the year, and rural states pick the Senate: Kansas, no Democratic senator since 1932, is a toss-up. 

That is 76 years before the Bitcoin whitepaper. Trump approval 33%, a record low.

NOT PRICED

6. Subpoenas arrive in January. Democrats take a chamber at 90%; first named targets are Trump family crypto ties and prediction markets, and Warren is favorite for Senate Banking chair. Apple, Microsoft and Palantir are hiring Democratic lobbyists now.

7. Ohio is the tell. A Fairshake affiliate spent $40m in 2024 to remove Sherrod Brown, four-year Banking chair. New polls put Brown ahead of Husted. Fairshake holds $122m and 32 endorsements, all House, 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats. $40m bought the first movie; nobody budgeted for the sequel. Money in the House, risk in the Senate.

8. The arithmetic. CLARITY lost at 49 with a 53-seat Republican Senate; it needed 60, so it needed Democrats either way. A flip changes the chairs, not the math. Today's rules are SEC and CFTC actions; a Democratic Congress cannot repeal what was never legislated.

9. The odds on prediction-market legislation are, fittingly, odd. $750m has traded on the midterms at Kalshi and Polymarket; Warren wants a public hearing on the venues and the CFTC wants the contracts called swaps. @icobeast should list a refund contract for the VCs who bought the pico top 😂 @0x_ultra can code it for him. 

10. The trade after the vote. A Democratic Congress against a hawkish Fed sets up spending and debt-ceiling fights in 2027 (Bloomberg). BTC trades the deficit, and the deficit gets decided there, not on Nov 3.

Post-midterms, crypto equities carry the January risk and the Warren risk; the coin carries the Fed and the fiscal fight after.

We find this out in January. One reason this epoch of Alpha strategies ends on January 15. We trade for what is not priced in. 🫡

quoted_text:
I was a lifelong Democrat. I thought most conservatives were ignorant or evil or lying. I believed almost everything written in the New York Times, The New Republic, and the Atlantic. I was horrified when conservatives criticized the authorities. Every criticism I saw: I thought all of it was motivated by animus, resentment, self-interest, or ignorance.

Whatever truth there might have been in the criticism, I saw as a mere "half-truth": an exploitation of this or that cherrypicked fact being weaponized. Why did I see it in terms of weaponization? Because I was biased: I saw liberal establishment institutions and figures as fundamentally good, so all criticism of them was automatically interpreted as being in bad faith.

Didn't the critics know that these institutions or figures were fundamentally good? If they didn't, they were ignorant. If they did, they were evil. It was that simple. This meant that any legitimate criticisms would just be dismissed, as if bouncing off of an impenetrable bulletproof shield.

This all changed once I started writing about the pandemic. Soon people started talking about me the way I once thought about conservatives. This led to a complete identity collapse as I came to understand that my old worldview was hateful and ignorant, that I hadn't understood what I had been judging.

I cannot forget the hearing that led to my dismissal from medical school a year after I started writing. During the hearing, people talked about me as if I wasn't human. My behavior was interpreted in the worst possible light. Complete fabrications were created. Nobody was concerned with the truth, only horrified at my apparent "unprofessional behavior", which was really a mirror of their unprofessional behavior directed at me. They structured the hearing to make it virtually impossible for me to speak and explain that what was being said was a lie. And nobody seemed to have any problem with this. Why? Because I was bad. If I am bad, then every mistreatment and every violation of the school's own policies became justified. A person who is bad does not deserve any rights. They only deserve punishment.

But the thing I remember most was the allusions to my social media activity. They said, "Kevin is driven by resentment from his childhood." I wasn't. I was on good terms with my parents. They alleged that I needed psychotherapy to deal with this trauma. It was a completely fake story that they had constructed about me, to demean me, to marginalize me, to try to explain the views I had expressed: that something terribly wrong had happened during the pandemic. They couldn't imagine that I might have legitimate points. So they reduced me to the same kinds of psychological caricatures that I once reduced conservatives to in my own mind.

When I was dismissed, I was broken. But I had help from friends who helped me understand what happened. And I came to realize that a hysteria had overtaken the left. I spent a lot of time reading about show trials, about witch trials, and so on. I also connected with people who had experienced similar things and came to realize that something similar had happened to hundreds of physicians around the country. My story wasn't unique. It was all the same story over and over again.

I cannot believe the person I once was. I cannot believe that I could exist like that. I still don't understand how I could be like that, or how millions of people in this country could continue being like that. It disturbs me greatly.

One thing I know is that whatever this thing is that is driving people crazy needs to be destroyed. It is hostile to civilization and to our humanity. It causes us to dehumanize each other and try to destroy each other. It is the very same monstrous thing that I once attributed to conservatives. But it had been inside me, and I could now see it inside others. This is something I still grapple with.

quoted_text:
i get asked VERY frequently to chat about data / RL envs / new companies coming into the space. all of the questions tend to be exactly the same so i want to summarize my thoughts: 

Q: "Should I start a data company?" 
A: probably not, unless you have some sort of alpha or have seen what frontier RL envs are like. basically, if you're not deep within an industry, seen data via a lab or working at another data company, or very well connected with lab researchers, you probably should not. though, if its your passion, now is the best time and it'll get increasingly worse. data is also much harder now than it was 6 months ago, and quality standards are ever-increasing. 

Q: "Is there a product in the space?" 
A: i think there are repeatable systems that can be created. i.e. QA systems, faster task generation, infrastructure around rollouts/VMs/GPU utilization/prod. system emulation etc. i think data is inherently bespoke, luckily LLMs allow you to harness bespoke intellect infinitely. i don't think it's a SaaS style product where it serves everyone immediately, but more of a quant-desk type system with alpha on how to do specific tasks embedded within an engineer-system like manner. each eng will have a desk that serves them specifically that unlocks 10x, 100x, 1000x capabilities. 

Q: "Is {insert set} data valuable"
A: depends on what you do with it. raw data dumps are cool but it's a lot more about what you can turn it into. 

Q: "How does {insert data company} differ from {insert competitor}?"
 OR 
"Should I join {insert data company}?"
A: if you're in the "big, legacy" data companies with contractors, it doesn't really differ that much. if i had to pick, i'd probably join mercor or surge from the big contractor companies, by virtue of early employees/founders being extremely smart. however, i'd much rather join a small, research-heavy data company. they are by far the companies with the highest slope. 

Q: "Won't labs just in-house this anyway?"
A: (1) data is an additive game that isn't zero-sum. just because labs are increasing synthetic data creation internally does not mean they won't buy more data. especially given it is an arms race to the top of intellect, if you can just make valuable data that moves the needle, it doesn't really matter if they can replicate it, it's not worth their researcher time if you solve a problem. the caveat being you have to actually add something yourself, and not just be a parrot who takes requests. saving researcher time is the name of the game. 
(2) i think this logic applies to everything, if you adopt this mentality, you probably should not work at any applied AI company, since they'll come after or absorb most products in the space.

Cloudflare 被我们中国网友称为“赛博菩萨”，因为它给的免费服务实在太多，让很多个人开发者和小网站省下了不少起步成本。

外国网友也在 X 上感叹：“Cloudflare 太好用、太便宜了，好到我都害怕哪天突然变卦。”

于是有人翻出了 CEO Matthew Prince 十年前的一篇旧回答：2016 年，他在 Stack Exchange 上解释，为什么 Cloudflare 会一直提供免费服务。

免费用户能帮助他们发现更多攻击、改进安全防护，也会把产品带进自己工作的公司；其中还有人会成为未来的员工。大量用户参与新功能测试，而网络规模扩大，又能降低带宽成本。免费服务本身，就能支撑这门生意。

但网友还是追问：这样的免费套餐，到底能持续多久？
结果 Prince 本人出现了，只回了一句：
“As long as I’m CEO.”
也就是：只要我还当 CEO，就会一直提供下去。

quoted_text:
I'm way less concerned about whether we're a little higher or lower in the next few weeks than where all the value will flow in the next few months.

I can stomach a dip to $75k on $BTC and 20%+ lower on alts. 

I can't stomach being sidelined for the on chain finance/tokeknization trend nearly a decade in the making.

You're not going to 10x your portfolio selling $BTC at $81k and buying $75k or buying $81k and selling $85k. Nobody has extreme macro edge here; we live in unpredictable, volatile, crazy times. If the vocal bears end up right, they'll have been sidelined since summer anyway and if the overlevered bulls are right, they'll still blow up eventually.

My only actionable advice is to shrink your bet sizing a little to take the volatility into account, eliminate the bloat and levered beta from your portfolio where you have no edge, and heavily concentrate into high conviction, idiosyncratic bets with near term catalysts. For me that looks like sizing down $BTC and even $HYPE exposure in favour of kinetiq:native for the upcoming Elysium launch, $AERO for the upcoming Aero multi-chain expansion, and $DRV for on chain options TAM expansion. Maybe for you it's $PRL and $NEAR. 

Very unpopular take, but $ZEC and $HYPE currently trade more like majors and levered beta than "idiosyncratic bets with near term catalysts that you have edge on". Doesn't make them bad long term investments at all, just don't feel the need to be overweight them at this time when they lack asymmetry. My example here would be if we're risk off, $HYPE could be $60 by EOY, and $100 if we're risk on. Pretty symmetric. kinetiq:native could be $0.15 if we're risk off, but it could be 5-10x higher if Elysium goes well. We want alts that behave like OTM calls, not 1.5x levered perps.

TLDR: Figure out where the next $1trn of value will flow on chain, place your bets (sized to survive), and let the macro LARPs chop each other up. The correctness of your allocations will more heavily dictate your 2027 performance than your current exposure level.

Jack Dorsey：如果比特币最终只是数字黄金，那它就是一个失败的项目！

我非常同意 @jack  这句话，而且我觉得他指出了比特币一个被很多人忽略的长期风险。

国家把 BTC 当储备、机构通过 ETF 疯狂买入，这些确实能推动价格上涨，但别忘了，中本聪白皮书的标题是《点对点电子现金系统》，比特币从诞生那天起，就不只是为了让大家囤币等升值。

还有一个更现实的问题：谁来长期支付比特币网络的安全成本？ 

矿工的收入只有两部分：区块补贴和链上交易手续费。

目前每个区块补贴 3.125 BTC，未来还会不断减半，最终趋近于零。

如果比特币只剩下囤积需求，缺乏足够的支付和结算活动，手续费无法弥补补贴下降，矿工收入和网络安全预算就可能持续承压。

这也是为什么我一直觉得，比特币必须同时具备数字黄金和全球支付结算网络两种属性。

比特币可以先成为数字黄金，但绝不能永远只是一块数字黄金。

text: what you should do is regularly do audit of your CLAUDE.md and SKILLS.md since after capability jump they drive models in the worse basin, models sometimes can do better without guidance, since your SKILL.md is training data
author: chiefofautism
quoted_text:
Delete your CLAUDE.md. Not edit it, not trim it, delete the whole file, along with your skills and your hooks, and see what the model does without them. That's Boris Cherny's actual advice from a recent YC appearance, and the Claude Code team has apparently followed it internally enough times that roughly 80% of their own system prompts are gone. His reasoning: most of those rules patched a weakness in whatever model you ran six or twelve months ago. Newer models often don't have that weakness anymore, so the instruction that used to help is now just constraining a more capable model for no reason. His method is almost embarrassingly plain. Delete everything, work normally for a while, watch where the model actually goes off track, add back exactly one instruction when a mistake repeats, and run the whole cycle again at the next major model release. Keep security and compliance rules. Keep the project quirks a model genuinely can't infer from reading the code. Cut folder structures, dependency lists, and architecture summaries, since a capable model can read those off the repo itself faster than it can read your stale description of them.

This is the same problem the rest of the field keeps rediscovering under different names. Anthropic's own long context guidance, OpenAI's notes on attention tradeoffs inside big windows, and Microsoft Research's GraphRAG papers all circle the same fact: a pile of context that only grows, whether it's a system prompt, a vector store, or a knowledge graph, degrades the thing using it, because stale facts sit next to current ones with no signal about which one wins. DeepSeek Harness takes a different structural swing at the same target, building its agent runtime out of swappable plugins so a stale capability gets replaced instead of buried under new instructions.

What strikes me is how little of this is about model capability and how much is housekeeping nobody assigned themselves. Most teams have a deprecation policy for their actual code. Almost nobody has one for the three paragraphs pasted into an agent's instructions eight months ago and never looked at again. How long is your CLAUDE.md, and when did you last delete anything from it?

The question is not if we will have a bear market, the question is if this administration can afford to let us have a bear market. 

- AI Capex is 50% of GDP. If it stops or slows down, GDP growth goes down the drain. No GDP growth = recession. Mainstreet gets hit the worst as the labor market will collapse. 

- 90% of consumer spending is done by the top 10%. They are levered against their assets that allow them to keep spending because their stocks keep going up. Stocks go down? Goodbye to consumer spending as we enter an actual recession given normal consumers already are borrowing from credit cards to pay for everything. 

- Social security will be wrecked over the coming 10 years. Why do you think we got the Trump Accounts? Because the administration believes in financial literacy? No, they need a replacement and having kids compound in the stock market to basically build their retirement account from birth could replace social security. That means stocks have to go up for those accounts to be worth anything and actually compound. Most 401Ks in this country are basically seen as retirement accounts. If the admin lets the market crash, people will not be able to afford retirement when social security benefits get cut into 2032. 

- We are $40T in debt. Bond yields continue to go higher which means the interest expense on our debt is approaching a significant part of our overall spending. The literal only way to solve this is cut spending or grow. Repubs or Dems will not cut spending…so growth is the only answer. If the market crashes, the chances of sustained growth in the greatest tech buildout we have ever seen will be impossible and ultimately make our debt situation even worse. We have to grow.

Not saying we can’t get into some horrible bear market, but given how levered the entire economy is to AI, which is basically the entire stock market, I do think this admin will try very hard to make sure we don’t have some horrible, ugly crash. If they let it happen, everything goes down the drain and the difference between now and dotcom is that demand for GPUs is very real (no oversupply) and the difference between now and 2008 is that the potential credit issue is not in housing and banks, it’s within GPUs and there is so much demand that the hyperscalers + Nvidia + the admin could come in to make sure things don’t get as bad as then. 

Maybe we could have some epic crash, but this administration really cannot afford to let that happen.

text:
Elon Musk explains why charging your EV to 100% on a road trip is a mistake:

On a road trip, your instinct is to fill the battery all the way up.

That's how you'd treat a gas tank.

But a battery doesn't work like a gas tank.

Charge to about 80%. Drive it down to 10% or less. Repeat.

This is just for long trips, when you want to spend as little time at the charger as possible.

Elon: "Getting from 80 to 100, it takes about as much time as getting from 0 to 80."

The reason is what's happening inside the battery.

Lithium ions travel from one side to the other, looking for a place to settle.

Think of them as cars hunting for a parking spot.

When the lot is empty, they zip right in.

As it fills up, they have to circle around, like at a packed mall.

So the closer the battery gets to full, the slower it charges.

The last few spots take the longest to find. https://t.co/a01e6cVSRq
